Article: a good answer has a title and an engaging opening, and answers the questions in the notice: why people keep pets (company, fun, responsibility), how animals help people (guide dogs, farm animals, making people less stressed) and a personal example (a family pet, a grandparent's horse). It should give opinions and reasons ('I believe that…', 'This is because…') and speak directly to the reader. Story: the story must begin with the given sentence and continue logically (why the dog was barking, what the writer discovered, how it ended). It needs a clear beginning, middle and end, a range of past tenses, some direct speech or description of feelings, and sequencing words ('At first', 'Then', 'In the end'). Both are marked for Content, Communicative Achievement, Organisation and Language.

questions.question:
Part 1 (2-3 minutes). The examiner asks you some questions about yourself.

What's your name? Where are you from?
Do you enjoy going shopping? Why / Why not?
Where do you usually buy your clothes?
Who do you like going shopping with?
Tell us about something you bought recently.
Do you prefer shopping online or in shops? Why?
questions.explanation: Answer each question with a short answer and then add a reason or an example: 'Yes, I love shopping, especially at weekends with my sister, because we always stop for a coffee too.' Use the present simple for habits ('I usually buy clothes at the shopping centre'), the past simple for recent purchases ('Last week I bought some new trainers because my old ones had a hole in them') and comparatives for preferences ('Shopping online is quicker, but in a shop you can try things on'). The examiner assesses Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management (extending answers), Pronunciation and Interactive Communication.

questions.question: Part 2 (about 1 minute). Look at the photograph. It shows a busy outdoor market. A man is selling fruit and vegetables from a stall, and a woman with a shopping bag is choosing some tomatoes. There are lots of other people walking between the stalls. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.
questions.explanation: Talk on your own for about one minute. Describe the place ('It's an outdoor market, maybe in a town square'), the people and what they are doing, using the present continuous ('A man is selling fruit', 'A woman is choosing some tomatoes'). Mention the colours, the different things on the stalls and the weather, and give your ideas about the situation ('I think it's Saturday morning because it's very busy', 'The fruit looks very fresh'). Useful language: 'At the front of the photo…', 'In the background there are…', 'It looks like…', 'Perhaps they're…'. If you don't know a word, describe it in other words ('the table where the man sells things'). Keep talking until the examiner says thank you.

questions.question:
Part 3 (2-3 minutes). Talk to your partner.

A friend of yours is moving to another city to start a new job, and you want to buy them a present. Here are some ideas:

a plant for their new flat
a photo album with pictures of your friends
a cookery book
a cinema voucher
a backpack
a map and guidebook of the new city

Talk together about the different presents you could buy, and say which would be the best one for your friend.
questions.explanation: This is a conversation with your partner, not a speech. Talk about each present, give your opinion with a reason and ask your partner what they think: 'A photo album would be lovely, because it will help them remember us. What do you think?' Think about your friend's situation: a new city, a new flat, a new job. Agree and disagree politely ('Good idea, but…', 'I'm not sure, because…') and make suggestions ('What about…?', 'Why don't we…?'). Near the end, try to reach a decision together: 'So, shall we buy the guidebook?' The examiner assesses how well you keep the conversation going and respond to your partner.

questions.question:
Part 4 (about 3 minutes). The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about shopping habits and saving money.

What kind of presents do you like to receive?
Do you think people spend too much money on things they don't need? Why / Why not?
Is it important for young people to save money? Why?
What are the best ways to save money?
Would you prefer to have a small shop in your street or a big shopping centre near your town? Why?
questions.explanation: Give full answers with reasons and examples, and react to what your partner says ('I agree with you, and also…', 'That's a good point, but…'). For example: 'I think saving money is very important, because one day you might want to buy a car or travel.' Use phrases for opinions ('In my opinion…', 'I think that…', 'On the other hand…'), 'should' for advice ('You should make a list before you go shopping') and 'would' for imaginary choices. The examiner assesses range of language, extending answers and interaction with your partner.

questions.question: Where are Nina and Chloe going to meet?
options: a) In a café
b) Outside the cinema
c) At the bus station
questions.explanation: Nina suggests "Why don't we meet in the café next door?" and Chloe agrees: "Good idea." They don't meet outside the cinema because of the rain, and Chloe will only travel from the bus station.

questions.question: What did Alex do last weekend?
options: a) He went to a festival.
b) He went camping.
c) He visited a museum.
questions.explanation: Alex says "we went to the transport museum". The camping was only "the plan", and the food festival "was cancelled because of the rain".

questions.question: Which tickets did Rachel buy?
options: a) A family ticket
b) One-day tickets
c) Tickets for a whole year
questions.explanation: Rachel says "So I got the tickets for the whole year." The family ticket is only for two adults and two children, and they are taking Chris's mum too. She thought the one-day tickets, "thirty pounds each", were too expensive.

questions.question: What does Ethan want to do this evening?
options: a) Watch a match on TV
b) Play a computer game
c) Go bowling
questions.explanation: Ethan says "the big match is on TV at eight, and I really want to see that". He can't go bowling because "I've only got five" pounds, and he is "bored" of the computer game.

questions.question: Where will the music festival be this year?
options: a) At a castle
b) By the river
c) On the beach
questions.explanation: The presenter says "this year it'll be in the grounds of Harwood Castle". The field by the river is "still too wet", and for the beach "the town council said no".

questions.question: What is Lily going to do on Saturday?
options: a) Go to a dance class
b) Go horse riding
c) Go to a birthday party
questions.explanation: Lily says "Grandma's already paid for the lesson, so I'll do that", meaning the riding lesson. There is no dance class "this week", and she will only "send Zara a present" instead of going to the party.

questions.question: How did Dan get his concert tickets?
options: a) At the box office
b) From a friend
c) On the website
questions.explanation: Dan says Tariq "won two in a radio competition" and "gave them to me". The website "kept crashing", and he only "thought about queuing at the box office".

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a gym. What problem does Olivia have with it?
options: a) It is a long way from her home.
b) It is too busy when she can go.
c) The equipment is quite old.
questions.explanation: Olivia says "I can only go after work, and that's when everyone else goes. I usually have to wait ages". The gym is "only five minutes from my flat" and the machines are "brand new".

questions.question: You will hear a boy talking to his mother about a running app. What does he think of the app?
options: a) It was too expensive to download.
b) It has made running more fun.
c) It makes running too hard.
questions.explanation: Max says he hated running, "But now it's like a game", and he is "trying to beat Lewis". The app "was free", and nothing suggests it makes running too hard.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about sleep. What do they agree about?
options: a) Using a phone in bed stops you sleeping.
b) Eight hours of sleep is too much.
c) Doing exercise during the day helps you sleep.
questions.explanation: Dominic looks at his phone in bed "and then I'm awake for ages", and Fiona says "Same here. I really think the screen keeps you awake." They disagree about exercise: swimming didn't help Dominic, but it helps Fiona.

questions.question: You will hear a girl telling a friend about yoga. Why did she start doing it?
options: a) Because her sister persuaded her
b) To make some new friends
c) To deal with stress
questions.explanation: Holly says "Exams, really. I was so stressed I couldn't think properly", and she tried yoga because it "helps you relax". Her sister asked her "for years", "but I always said no", so that wasn't the reason.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about cycling to work. What is Ian's opinion of it?
options: a) It is dangerous on the busy roads in town.
b) It makes him feel tired.
c) It is quicker than driving.
questions.explanation: Ian says "with all the traffic in the mornings, I actually get there ten minutes earlier" than by car. It is Kirsty who thinks it is dangerous; Ian feels "quite safe" and is "not tired at all".

questions.question: You will hear a man talking about giving up sugar. How does he feel about it now?
options: a) He is surprised it has been so easy.
b) He is upset that he hasn't lost weight.
c) He misses sweet food a lot.
questions.explanation: Pete "was sure I'd be desperate for chocolate", "But honestly, I hardly think about it." He hasn't lost weight, but "that wasn't really why I did it", so he is not upset about it.

questions.question: Number of places to collect a bike when the scheme starts: ____
questions.explanation: Gareth says 'To begin with, there'll be fifteen places around Hadley where you can collect a bike'. Thirty is the number the council hopes to have by next summer.

questions.question: You can register online or at the ____ on Market Street.
questions.explanation: Gareth says you can register 'online, or, if you'd rather speak to someone, at the library on Market Street'. He says 'you can't register' at the town hall.

questions.question: After the free period, you pay £1 for each ____.
questions.explanation: Gareth says 'The first thirty minutes of every journey are free. After that, you pay one pound for each hour'.

questions.question: Every bike has a ____ at the front, which is useful for shopping.
questions.explanation: Gareth says 'every one has a basket at the front, which is really useful if you're going shopping'. The bikes also have lights, but these are for riding after dark.

questions.question: You can buy a cheap helmet at the cycle shop inside the ____.
questions.explanation: Gareth says 'you can buy a cheap one at the cycle shop inside the railway station'. The council itself does not provide helmets.

questions.question: To report a problem with a bike, press the ____ button on the stand.
questions.explanation: Gareth says to 'press the red button. That tells our team it needs repairing.' The green button is 'only for unlocking the bike'.

questions.question: Why did Priya decide to move to Chile?
options: a) She wanted to be with her partner.
b) She wanted a change from her old routine.
c) She was offered a higher salary there.
questions.explanation: Priya says 'I'd simply been doing the same job in the same school for five years, and I felt I needed something new.' She says 'I earn less now', and 'I didn't follow a boyfriend there'.

questions.question: What did Priya find hardest when she first arrived?
options: a) Understanding how things worked at school
b) Finding her way around a new city
c) Learning to speak Spanish well enough to teach
questions.explanation: Priya says 'What I found difficult was all the unwritten rules at school', such as 'how formally I should speak to the head teacher'. She expected the language to be a problem, but her Spanish 'improved quite quickly'.

questions.question: What does Priya say about her students in Chile?
options: a) Their English is better than she expected.
b) They worry less about getting things wrong.
c) They behave very differently from teenagers at home.
questions.explanation: Priya says her students 'are much less afraid of making mistakes. They'll just start speaking, even if their English isn't perfect.' She says they are 'not that different, really' from teenagers in England.

questions.question: What is Priya's opinion of the way her Chilean colleagues teach?
options: a) She still believes her own methods are better.
b) It is very similar to teaching in the UK.
c) She has learnt useful things from it.
questions.explanation: Priya says 'We've learnt a lot from each other, and I've completely changed some of my lessons because of them.' She thought her way was better 'At first', but says 'I've changed my mind.'

questions.question: How does Priya feel about being far from her family?
options: a) She may go back to England because of it.
b) She finds it difficult for most of the year.
c) It is less difficult than she expected.
questions.explanation: Priya says 'it's been much easier than I feared.' It is only 'really hard' at Christmas, not for most of the year, and she never talks about going back.

questions.question: What is Priya's main advice to teachers who want to work abroad?
options: a) Plan to stay for at least two years.
b) Learn the language perfectly before going.
c) Choose a school in a large city.
questions.explanation: Priya says 'My main advice would be to stay for at least two years.' She disagrees with people who say 'you should learn the language perfectly before you go'.

questions.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Campers can't drive in or out late at night.
b) Campers must be inside their tents by 10.30 pm.
c) Cars must be parked outside the campsite at night.
questions.explanation: Between 10.30 pm and 7 am 'The gate is locked … so cars cannot enter or leave the site'. Cars are not sent outside the site – they just cannot move in or out – and the sign only asks for no music or loud voices, not for people to be in their tents.

questions.question: What does the note tell guests?
options: a) All food in the fridge is removed every Monday.
b) They can take any food they find in the fridge.
c) They should write their departure date on their food.
questions.explanation: Guests must label food 'with your name and the date you are leaving'. Only the free shelf is for everyone – not the whole fridge – and only 'food without a label' is thrown away on Mondays, not all food.

questions.question: Why has Ellie sent this message?
options: a) To ask Tom to buy a new torch on the way
b) To warn Tom not to go near the river
c) To tell Tom where to find her
questions.explanation: Ellie explains that they are 'in the top field next to the shower block' and tells Tom to 'Look for the green tent', so she is telling him where they are. She asks him to 'Bring a torch', not to buy one, and she mentions the flooded field only to explain why they moved.

questions.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) The price of a bed includes the use of a towel.
b) Guests should leave their sheets in a basket.
c) Guests need to bring their own sheets.
questions.explanation: The sign says 'please put your used sheets in the basket by the front door' on the day you leave. Sheets are 'included in the price', so guests do not bring their own, but towels cost '£2' extra, so they are not included.

questions.question: What should Ms Lindqvist do if she will arrive after 8 pm?
options: a) Wait at the gate until someone comes
b) Phone the campsite earlier that day
c) Collect her welcome pack from reception
questions.explanation: The email says 'If you expect to arrive later, call us before 6 pm'. Reception is closed after 8 pm, so she cannot collect the pack there – it will be 'in the box by the gate' – and the email does not say that anyone will come to the gate.

questions.question: Zara is 17 and hopes to become a vet one day, so she wants to get some experience of working with animals. She is at school all week, so she can only help at weekends.
options: A) Clean Parks Day
B) Digital Buddies
C) Willow Farm Animal Sanctuary
D) Brightstart Homework Club
E) Greenway Community Garden
F) Happy Paws Dog Rescue
G) Riverside 10K Run
H) Northgate Welcome Centre
questions.explanation: At Willow Farm Animal Sanctuary volunteers 'feed the animals' and 'sometimes assist our vet', it accepts people 'aged 16 and over', and it is open 'on Saturdays and Sundays'. Happy Paws Dog Rescue also works with animals, but volunteers 'must be at least 18' and come 'on a weekday'.

questions.question: Brian has just retired and would like to spend time outdoors growing things. He's hoping to meet new people, and he'd prefer to help on weekday mornings.
options: A) Clean Parks Day
B) Digital Buddies
C) Willow Farm Animal Sanctuary
D) Brightstart Homework Club
E) Greenway Community Garden
F) Happy Paws Dog Rescue
G) Riverside 10K Run
H) Northgate Welcome Centre
questions.explanation: At Greenway Community Garden volunteers 'dig, plant and harvest', there's 'a friendly chat over a cup of tea', and they meet 'on Tuesday and Thursday mornings'. Clean Parks Day is also outdoors, includes planting bulbs and is a way to 'make new friends', but it takes place on Saturdays.

questions.question: Leila grew up speaking Arabic and French and would like to use her languages to help adults who are new to the country. She works during the day, so she is only free in the evenings.
options: A) Clean Parks Day
B) Digital Buddies
C) Willow Farm Animal Sanctuary
D) Brightstart Homework Club
E) Greenway Community Garden
F) Happy Paws Dog Rescue
G) Riverside 10K Run
H) Northgate Welcome Centre
questions.explanation: Northgate Welcome Centre supports 'families who have recently arrived in this country', wants volunteers who speak 'Arabic, French or Farsi', and is open 'on Monday and Wednesday evenings'. Brightstart Homework Club also welcomes volunteers who speak Arabic, but it helps children, not adults, and it runs on Wednesday afternoons.

questions.question: Sam is a university student who is very good with computers. He'd like to use his skills to help older people, and he has no lectures on Wednesday afternoons.
options: A) Clean Parks Day
B) Digital Buddies
C) Willow Farm Animal Sanctuary
D) Brightstart Homework Club
E) Greenway Community Garden
F) Happy Paws Dog Rescue
G) Riverside 10K Run
H) Northgate Welcome Centre
questions.explanation: Digital Buddies helps 'older people' who don't know how to use a smartphone, needs volunteers 'who are good with technology', and meets 'every Wednesday afternoon'. Brightstart Homework Club also teaches 'computer skills' on Wednesday afternoons, but it is for 'children aged 7 to 11', not older people.

questions.question: Nadia loves sport and would like to help at a big event. She can't promise to volunteer regularly, so she's looking for something that only takes one day.
options: A) Clean Parks Day
B) Digital Buddies
C) Willow Farm Animal Sanctuary
D) Brightstart Homework Club
E) Greenway Community Garden
F) Happy Paws Dog Rescue
G) Riverside 10K Run
H) Northgate Welcome Centre
questions.explanation: The Riverside 10K Run needs volunteers for 'an exciting sporting event', and 'It's just one day'. Clean Parks Day is also something she could do on a single day, but it means picking up litter and planting in a park, not helping at a sports event.

questions.question: What often surprises people about the mountain rescue team?
options: a) How quickly its members can get to the base
b) That its members receive no money for their work
c) That it is organised and paid for by the government
d) How many times it is called out every year
questions.explanation: Rhys says the volunteers are not paid: 'none of them is paid. People are often amazed when I tell them that.' People wrongly 'imagine we're professionals working for the government', and the team actually 'depends on money from the public'. The number of call-outs and the ten-minute journey are facts in the text, but nothing says they surprise people.

questions.question: Why did Rhys decide to join the team?
options: a) He wanted to improve his own skills in the mountains.
b) He was grateful for the way the team had helped him.
c) A friend who was already a member asked him to join.
d) He felt embarrassed that he was not fit enough.
questions.explanation: When Rhys was lost, 'The team found me in about an hour, and they didn't make me feel stupid at all. I decided I wanted to do the same for other people.' He is embarrassed about going up 'in trainers, without a map', not about his fitness, and no friend or wish to improve his own skills is mentioned.

questions.question: What did Rhys find most difficult during his training?
options: a) The physical effort of carrying people down
b) Learning how to find his way in the dark
c) The comments he got from the older members
d) Finding enough free time to study first aid
questions.explanation: Rhys says: 'I thought I was fit, but carrying a heavy stretcher down a steep hill in the rain is something else. I was always the slowest.' Finding the way at night and first aid are part of the training, but he does not say they were hard, and the older members 'never criticised him'.

questions.question: What is Rhys's opinion about people who go walking in the mountains?
options: a) Fewer people should go there because it is dangerous.
b) Walkers should stop sharing photos on social media.
c) Only experienced walkers should try to climb the high mountains.
d) Anyone can go if they take the right things with them.
questions.explanation: Rhys 'doesn't want people to stay away' and says: 'We'd much rather people came well prepared, with warm clothes, a map and a charged phone, than not at all.' He thinks social media is 'partly responsible' for more call-outs, but he does not ask people to stop posting, and he never says only experienced walkers should go.

questions.question: What is the writer mainly trying to do in this article?
options: a) Describe how one injured walker was rescued at night
b) Explain why rescue teams need more money
c) Show what life is like for a rescue volunteer
d) Give advice on staying safe in the mountains
questions.explanation: The article follows Rhys from the call during dinner, through his reasons for joining and his training, to opening 'his shop as usual at nine' after a night rescue, so it shows what being a volunteer involves. The October rescue, money from the public and safety equipment are each mentioned only briefly as part of his story.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (1)?
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.
questions.explanation: 'It was then' refers to the evening when Sophie counted the plastic, 'it' means plastic, and the decision made by 'she and her husband' contrasts with the next sentence: 'Their two children… were much less enthusiastic.' The sentence saying the children were 'delighted' contradicts 'much less enthusiastic'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (2)?
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.
questions.explanation: Because the supermarket's food 'came wrapped in plastic', the family went to 'the weekly market' with 'their own bags and boxes'. The next sentence, 'Some of the stallholders found this strange', needs the market to have been mentioned. The sentence saying the supermarket had stopped selling food in plastic contradicts 'Almost everything in their usual supermarket came wrapped in plastic'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (3)?
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.
questions.explanation: 'This' is the problem of shampoo and toothpaste in 'plastic bottles', and 'some of them' are those products. Making them herself leads to the next sentence: 'Her homemade toothpaste, she admits, was not a success.' No other sentence explains why her toothpaste was 'homemade'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (4)?
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.
questions.explanation: 'On the other hand' contrasts the extra time ('four extra hours a week') with a benefit, and saving money leads to the next sentence: 'their food bills had fallen by almost a fifth.' The sentence saying cooking 'took hardly any time at all' contradicts 'Living without plastic also took a lot of time'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (5)?
options: A) On the other hand, they saved money, because they stopped buying ready meals and snacks.
B) It was then that she and her husband, Dan, decided to try living without it for a whole year.
C) The children were delighted and helped to plan every detail.
D) Luckily, their local supermarket had already stopped selling food in plastic.
E) So the family started doing their shopping at the weekly market in Norwich, taking their own bags and boxes.
F) Cooking every meal from fresh ingredients, however, took hardly any time at all.
G) Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits.
H) Sophie solved this by learning to make some of them herself, using recipes she found online.
questions.explanation: After the good result, 'Even the children now refuse to go back to their old habits', and the next sentence gives an example: 'Leo, who complained the most at the beginning, now gives talks about it.' The sentence saying the children were delighted from the start contradicts 'complained the most at the beginning'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (1).
options: a) went
b) made
c) set
d) put
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "go on sale", meaning become available to buy: the phone "went on sale in the United States". 'Put on sale' would need a passive ('was put on sale'), and 'made' or 'set on sale' are not used.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (2).
options: a) alone
b) single
c) unique
d) only
questions.explanation: The battery "lasted for only thirty minutes": 'only' goes before a number to show it is small. 'Alone', 'single' and 'unique' cannot be used before 'thirty minutes' in this way.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (3).
options: a) contain
b) belong
c) involve
d) consist
questions.explanation: Each message "could only contain up to 160 characters", meaning it could have no more than 160 letters and symbols in it. 'Consist' and 'belong' need a preposition (consist of, belong to), and 'involve' means 'include as a necessary activity', which does not fit characters in a message.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (4).
options: a) spending
b) using
c) making
d) doing
questions.explanation: People could "search the internet without using a computer", because the phone itself did the job. 'Making a computer' means building one, and 'doing' or 'spending a computer' are not possible.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (5).
options: a) made
b) given
c) put
d) taken
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "take the place of", meaning replace: smartphones "had taken the place of cameras, maps and even alarm clocks". 'Given', 'put' and 'made the place of' are not English expressions.

questions.question: Choose the correct word for gap (6).
options: a) believe
b) wonder
c) imagine
d) think
questions.explanation: "It is hard to imagine life without these clever little machines" means it is difficult to picture life with no phones. 'Think' and 'wonder' need a preposition or clause ('think about', 'wonder what…'), and 'believe life without' does not make sense.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (1).
questions.explanation: By midnight points to a time in the past, so the past perfect is needed: "by midnight we had still not found him anywhere". Have would need a present time.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (2).
questions.explanation: With a perfect tense, 'since' introduces the point in time when something started: "Biscuit had been missing since Sunday evening". 'For' is used with a period of time (for four days), not with a point like 'Sunday evening'.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (3).
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'give up hope' means stop believing something good will happen: after four days "we were starting to give up hope".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (4).
questions.explanation: The comparison 'as + adverb + as' needs a second 'as': "I ran next door as fast as I could".

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (5).
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'so + adjective + that' to show a result: Biscuit was "so thin that I hardly recognised him". 'Such' is not possible before an adjective without a noun, and 'too' cannot be followed by 'that'.

questions.question: Write ONE word for gap (6).
questions.explanation: The pattern 'It wasn't until … that …' shows that something happened only after another event: "It wasn't until he had eaten two bowls of food that he finally began to purr." 'Till' has the same meaning and is also accepted.

questions.question:
Part 1. You must answer this question.

Read this email from your friend Ella and the notes you have made.

From: Ella
Subject: Our camping trip

Hi!

I've found a lovely campsite next to a lake for our trip on the weekend of 22 May. It's got a shop and a café, and you can hire canoes there! [Note 1: Sounds great!]

We can get there by train and walk from the station, or we can cycle all the way. It's about 30 kilometres. Which do you prefer? [Note 2: Say which and why]

We need to take some food for cooking on the campfire. What should we take? [Note 3: Suggest …]

My tent is quite small. Have you got a bigger one? [Note 4: No, but …]

Love,
Ella

Write your email to Ella using all the notes. Write about 100 words.
questions.explanation: A good answer is an informal email to a friend (e.g. 'Hi Ella,' … 'Can't wait!') of about 100 words that deals with all four notes: (1) reacts positively to the campsite ('That sounds great! I've always wanted to try canoeing'); (2) chooses the train or cycling and gives a reason ('I'd rather take the train because our bags will be heavy' / 'Let's cycle, it'll be fun and it's cheaper'); (3) suggests some food ('We could take sausages and bread, and some marshmallows'); (4) says the writer has no bigger tent but offers a solution ('No, but my cousin has a big one and I'm sure she'll lend it to us'). Marks are given for Content (all four notes), Communicative Achievement (friendly, enthusiastic tone), Organisation (paragraphs and linking words) and Language (B1 structures such as 'I'd rather…', 'We could…', 'will' for offers and predictions). Missing a note reduces the Content mark.

questions.question:
Part 2. Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2: Article
You see this notice in an English-language travel magazine.

ARTICLES WANTED!
A weekend in the countryside
Where would you go for a weekend in the countryside? What would you do there? Why do some people prefer the countryside to the city?
Write an article answering these questions. The best article will win a prize.

Write your article.

Question 3: Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
'We could hear something moving outside the tent.'

Write your story.
questions.explanation: Candidates answer only ONE question, in about 100 words. Article: a good answer has a title and an interesting opening, and answers the questions in the notice: a place in the countryside (mountains, a farm, a village near a river), activities there (walking, fishing, riding a bike, having a picnic) and reasons why some people prefer the countryside (fresh air, peace and quiet, nature). It should give opinions, compare the countryside with the city ('It's much quieter than…') and speak directly to the reader. Story: the story must begin with the given sentence and develop it (what the noise was, how the characters felt, what they did, how it ended, perhaps with a funny or surprising ending). It needs a clear beginning, middle and end, past tenses used correctly (past simple and past continuous), and sequencing words ('Suddenly', 'A moment later', 'In the end'). Both are marked for Content, Communicative Achievement, Organisation and Language.

questions.question:
Part 1 (2-3 minutes). The examiner asks you some questions about yourself.

What's your name? Do you work or are you a student?
How often do you use your mobile phone?
What do you use the internet for?
Which app do you use most? Why?
Tell us about the first computer or phone you had.
Do you like playing computer games? Why / Why not?
questions.explanation: Answer each question with a short answer and then add a reason or an example: 'I use my phone all the time, mostly to send messages to my friends and listen to music on the bus.' Use the present simple for habits ('I usually check my messages in the morning'), the past simple for the past ('My first phone was my mum's old one, and it was very slow') and give reasons with 'because'. The examiner assesses Grammar and Vocabulary, Discourse Management (extending answers), Pronunciation and Interactive Communication.

questions.question: Part 2 (about 1 minute). Look at the photograph. It shows a grandmother and two teenagers sitting together on a sofa in a living room. One of the teenagers is holding a tablet and showing her something on the screen, and they are all laughing. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.
questions.explanation: Talk on your own for about one minute. Say where the people are ('They're in a living room, maybe at the grandmother's house'), who they are and what they are doing, using the present continuous ('One of the teenagers is holding a tablet', 'They're all laughing'). Describe details such as the furniture, their clothes and their faces, and guess about the situation ('Perhaps they're watching a funny video', 'I think the teenagers are teaching their grandmother how to use the tablet'). Useful language: 'On the left / right…', 'Next to her…', 'It looks as if…', 'They might be…'. If you don't know a word, describe it in other words. Keep talking until the examiner says thank you.

questions.question:
Part 3 (2-3 minutes). Talk to your partner.

A family wants to spend a whole weekend without phones, computers or television. Here are some things they could do instead:

play board games
go for a bike ride
bake a cake together
visit a museum
camp in the garden
learn to play a musical instrument

Talk together about the different things the family could do, and say which would be the most enjoyable for the whole family.
questions.explanation: This is a conversation with your partner, not a speech. Talk about each activity, give your opinion with a reason and ask your partner what they think: 'Baking a cake is a good idea because everyone can help, and then you can eat it! What do you think?' Remember the family has people of different ages, and they must not use screens. Agree and disagree politely ('I see what you mean, but…', 'I'm not so sure about that…') and make suggestions ('What about…?', 'They could…'). Near the end, try to reach a decision together: 'So, do we agree on camping in the garden?' The examiner assesses how well you keep the conversation going and respond to your partner.

questions.question:
Part 4 (about 3 minutes). The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about technology and free time.

What do you like doing in your free time when you are not using a screen?
Do you think people spend too much time on their phones? Why / Why not?
How has technology changed the way families spend time together?
Is it a good idea to learn new skills from online videos? Why / Why not?
Would you find it difficult to live without the internet for a week? Why?
questions.explanation: Give full answers with reasons and examples, and react to what your partner says ('I agree with you, because…', 'Really? I think…'). For example: 'I think technology has made families talk less, because everyone looks at their own phone during dinner.' Use phrases for opinions ('In my opinion…', 'I believe that…', 'On the other hand…'), the present perfect for changes ('Technology has changed…') and 'would' for imaginary situations ('It would be hard, but I'd read more books'). The examiner assesses range of language, extending answers and interaction with your partner.

questions.question: What has the woman bought for her brother’s birthday?
options: a) Some headphones
b) A board game
c) A football shirt
questions.explanation: The woman says "in the end I got him some headphones". She wanted a football shirt, but "they didn’t have his size", and the board game is the present their mum has bought.

questions.question: What is the man going to buy for his colleague?
options: a) A recipe book
b) A small plant
c) Some flowers
questions.explanation: The man says "I’ll get her a little plant for her new office". He rejects flowers because "they’ll be dead in a week", and Rachel already has "hundreds" of recipe books.

questions.question: How much did the woman pay for the scarf?
questions.explanation: The label said £30 and the sale price was £24, but the assistant "took another six pounds off", and the man checks: "So you paid eighteen pounds?"

questions.question: When is the man taking his parents out for a meal?
options: a) On Saturday evening
b) On Sunday lunchtime
c) On Friday evening
questions.explanation: The man says "we’re going for lunch on Sunday". Friday is not possible because his dad works until nine, and on Saturday evening "the restaurant was fully booked".

questions.question: What are they going to make for their grandmother?
options: a) A birthday card
b) A birthday cake
c) A photo album
questions.explanation: The man suggests "putting some old family photos into an album" and the woman agrees: "she’d love that". Auntie Sue is already making the cake, and "She’ll get lots of cards".

questions.question: Which bag does the woman decide to buy for her friend?
options: a) A striped beach bag
b) A black backpack
c) A brown leather bag
questions.explanation: The woman says "she’d like the brown leather one best" and does not mind the price. Lucy is not "a beach person", and she has "just bought" a backpack.

questions.question: What time does the store close this week?
options: a) At half past five
b) At six o’clock
c) At seven o’clock
questions.explanation: This week "the store is staying open until seven o’clock". Half past five is the "normal closing time", and six is when only the gift-wrapping desk closes.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a running app. What does the man think of it?
options: a) It helps him to keep going.
b) It is still hard for him to use.
c) It costs too much for what it does.
questions.explanation: The man says "without it I’d have stopped running weeks ago" and that it makes him "want to go out again". It isn’t free, but it’s "worth every penny", and the buttons were only difficult at first: "now it’s easy".

questions.question: You will hear a woman telling a friend about a video call with her grandparents. How did she feel about it?
options: a) Bored because it went on so long
b) Pleased that it was so easy
c) Worried that they couldn’t hear her
questions.explanation: She expected problems, but "it worked first time" and "it was the best part of my week". She "could hear them perfectly", and chatting "for ages" was a pleasure, not boring.

questions.question: You will hear two colleagues talking about a new booking system at work. What do they agree about?
options: a) It will save them time in the end.
b) Staff should have had training first.
c) It is slower than the old system.
questions.explanation: The man says "They should have given us a proper course before it started" and the woman replies "I agree". She thinks it is "better than the old one", and the man is "not so sure" it will save time.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a language app. Why did the woman stop using it?
options: a) She had to pay for it.
b) The games were too easy.
c) It didn’t help her to speak.
questions.explanation: In Valencia she "couldn’t have a single conversation", so now she goes to a class "where we actually talk". The app is free ("It is"), and she says "the games were fun".

questions.question: You will hear a woman talking to a friend about an evening without phones. What is her opinion of it?
options: a) It was better than she expected.
b) It was a good idea but too long.
c) It was hard for her children.
questions.explanation: She says "I thought I’d hate it", but they "laughed all evening" and will "do it every Friday now". Her kids "didn’t even ask for their phones", and she never says it was too long.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a smart watch. Why did the man buy it?
options: a) Because it looks fashionable
b) To read his messages more easily
c) To check how much he sleeps
questions.explanation: He says "I wanted to know how many hours I really get each night". His phone is "fine" for messages, and the good looks are "just a bonus".

questions.question: The theatre building was first used as a ____.
questions.explanation: Helen says visitors think it was a church, "but in fact it was built as a fish market". The church is only what people wrongly believe.

questions.question: Number of seats in the theatre today: ____
questions.explanation: Twelve hundred was the number when the theatre first opened; Helen then says "today we have eight hundred and fifty seats".

questions.question: Colour of the ceiling: ____, with gold stars
questions.explanation: People "expect a theatre ceiling to be red, but ours is green, with little gold stars". Red is what visitors expect, not the real colour.

questions.question: The workshop downstairs is where the ____ are made.
questions.explanation: "Down these stairs is the workshop where the costumes are made." The wigs are not made there: "We order those from a company in London."

questions.question: On the stage, visitors must not touch the ____.
questions.explanation: Visitors may walk around and sit on the furniture, but Helen asks "that you don’t touch the ropes at the side of the stage".

questions.question: Show your ticket in the ____ to get ten per cent off.
questions.explanation: "If you show it in the café on the ground floor, you’ll get ten per cent off". The discount "doesn’t work in the gift shop".

questions.question: Why did Megan leave her job at the bank?
options: a) She was only really happy when baking.
b) She did not get on with her colleagues.
c) She was not earning enough money there.
questions.explanation: Megan says "Saturday mornings in the kitchen were the only time I felt really happy". Money and colleagues were not the reason: "The pay was fine and my colleagues were lovely".

questions.question: How did Megan feel on the day her shop opened?
options: a) Afraid that no customers would come
b) Worried that her bread was not good enough
c) Excited about trying out new recipes
questions.explanation: She was "terrified" and kept thinking "what if … nobody comes through the door?" She was not worried about her bread: "I knew my bread was good."

questions.question: What does Megan say about starting work very early?
options: a) She would like to start later in the day.
b) It is not as bad as people told her.
c) It is the hardest part of being a baker.
questions.explanation: "Everyone warned me it would be awful, but actually I don’t mind it at all." The thing she finds hard is "going to bed at nine", not the early start.

questions.question: What does Megan think is most important in a bakery?
options: a) Recipes that no other shop uses
b) Baking everything perfectly every single day
c) Staff who make customers feel welcome
questions.explanation: "For me, it’s the people behind the counter. If customers feel welcome, if you remember their names …". She says recipes "matter" but are not the most important thing, and customers return "even on a day when the croissants aren’t perfect".

questions.question: What is Megan’s attitude towards supermarkets?
options: a) She is worried because their prices are lower.
b) She does not see them as real competition.
c) She thinks the bread they sell is poor.
questions.explanation: "I don’t think we’re really competing." She says supermarket bread can be "perfectly nice", and although it is cheaper, she answers "Not really" when asked if that worries her.

questions.question: What advice does Megan give to young people?
options: a) Read as many business books as you can.
b) Wait until all your plans are perfect.
c) Get some practical experience first.
questions.explanation: "Do get some experience first." She says the opposite of waiting ("Don’t wait until everything is perfect") and learned more in a shop "than from any book".

questions.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) Mirrors must be taken to another area.
b) Bottles and jars must be washed before you recycle them.
c) Window glass should go in the green containers.
questions.explanation: The notice says the centre can "no longer accept window glass or mirrors" and asks people to "take these to the general waste area", so mirrors go somewhere else. Window glass is exactly what the green containers no longer take, and the notice asks people to remove lids, not to wash bottles.

questions.question: Why has Priya written to Tom?
options: a) To suggest meeting at a café before they start
b) To give him the correct start time
c) To ask him to bring bags for everyone
questions.explanation: Priya writes that the clean-up "starts at 9, not 10 as it says on the poster", so she is correcting the time Tom has seen. Bags are already "provided", so Tom does not need to bring them, and she says "there’s no café nearby", so she is not suggesting meeting at one.

questions.question: What does the sign tell people?
options: a) Food waste may be put in this bin with the card.
b) All cardboard boxes should be thrown in the black bin.
c) Pizza boxes that are dirty must not go in this bin.
questions.explanation: The sign says "Pizza boxes with food on them cannot be recycled and should go in the black bin instead", so dirty pizza boxes must not go in the paper bin. The bin is for "PAPER AND CARD ONLY", so food is not allowed, and clean boxes go in this bin once they are flattened, not in the black bin.

questions.question: Why should people sign up before Thursday?
options: a) So that each child can be given an adult to work with
b) So that the organisers know how much lunch to get
c) Because only a small number of volunteers can join
questions.explanation: The notice asks people to sign up "by Thursday so that we can order enough food" for the "free lunch". Nothing limits the number of volunteers, and children "must come with an adult" – the organisers do not find one for them.

questions.question: What is the email about?
options: a) Residents should put their bins out on Monday morning.
b) Garden waste will no longer be collected after this week.
c) Next week, bins will be collected a day late.
questions.explanation: The email says "all bin collections next week will be one day later than usual" because of the bank holiday. Garden waste stops only for one week, as "Normal collections start again the week after", and Monday is mentioned only as the bank holiday, not as a collection day.

questions.question: Gwen wants to take her elderly father for a walk of no more than two hours. He can’t manage hills or steps, and they’d like to have something to eat when they finish.
options: A) Clifftop Sunrise Walk
B) Woodland and Waterfall Walk
C) Heron Marsh Nature Reserve
D) Castle Bay Promenade
E) Three Tops Challenge
F) Riverside Mill Trail
G) Plas Hendre Deer Park
H) Cadair Summit Day
questions.explanation: The Riverside Mill Trail is "completely flat", "takes around an hour and a half" and "finishes at the old mill, now a tea room serving light lunches". The Woodland and Waterfall Walk is short and has a café, but "The path climbs steeply in places" and there are "120 steps", which her father cannot manage.

questions.question: Rhys and his children, aged 8 and 10, love spotting birds and animals. They want to bring their dog, and as they don’t have a car, they need a walk they can get to by bus or train.
options: A) Clifftop Sunrise Walk
B) Woodland and Waterfall Walk
C) Heron Marsh Nature Reserve
D) Castle Bay Promenade
E) Three Tops Challenge
F) Riverside Mill Trail
G) Plas Hendre Deer Park
H) Cadair Summit Day
questions.explanation: At Heron Marsh "The number 42 bus stops right at the entrance", visitors can "watch herons, otters" and ducklings, and "Dogs on leads are welcome on all paths". Plas Hendre Deer Park has deer and is near a station, but "dogs are not allowed in the park".

questions.question: Fiona is an experienced walker who wants to spend a whole day in the mountains and enjoy the views from the top. She’d prefer to walk with other people and someone who knows the way.
options: A) Clifftop Sunrise Walk
B) Woodland and Waterfall Walk
C) Heron Marsh Nature Reserve
D) Castle Bay Promenade
E) Three Tops Challenge
F) Riverside Mill Trail
G) Plas Hendre Deer Park
H) Cadair Summit Day
questions.explanation: Cadair Summit Day is "a seven-hour climb to the top" with views "all the way to Ireland from the summit", and walkers go in "Groups of up to ten" with "one of our experienced guides". The Three Tops Challenge is a long mountain day with great views, but there is no guide: "you must be able to use a map and compass".

questions.question: Owen enjoys taking photos of the sea early in the morning, just as the sun comes up. He wants a walk where he won’t meet many other people.
options: A) Clifftop Sunrise Walk
B) Woodland and Waterfall Walk
C) Heron Marsh Nature Reserve
D) Castle Bay Promenade
E) Three Tops Challenge
F) Riverside Mill Trail
G) Plas Hendre Deer Park
H) Cadair Summit Day
questions.explanation: The Clifftop Sunrise Walk is a coastal path that is "at its best at dawn", and if you set off early "you’ll probably have the path to yourself". Castle Bay Promenade also follows the sea, but "It’s one of the busiest paths in the area".

questions.question: Mei is going for a walk with a friend who uses a wheelchair, so they need a path with a smooth surface. They would also like to learn something about the history of the area.
options: A) Clifftop Sunrise Walk
B) Woodland and Waterfall Walk
C) Heron Marsh Nature Reserve
D) Castle Bay Promenade
E) Three Tops Challenge
F) Riverside Mill Trail
G) Plas Hendre Deer Park
H) Cadair Summit Day
questions.explanation: On Castle Bay Promenade "The surface is smooth all the way, so it suits wheelchairs", and "boards along the route tell the story of the castle and its battles". Plas Hendre Deer Park has a "seventeenth-century country house", but its paths "are not suitable for wheelchairs".

questions.question: Why did Josh leave his college course?
options: a) He had already opened his own shop.
b) He found the work far too difficult.
c) He wanted to do more practical work.
d) He needed to earn money for his family.
questions.explanation: Josh says: "The course was mostly theory. I wanted to work with real machines." He wanted practical work. The text never says the course was too difficult, and he opened the shop only later, after a year of repairs in the garage.

questions.question: Why did Josh stop working in his parents’ garage?
options: a) He wanted to be closer to the university.
b) His mother asked him to find somewhere else.
c) His customers could not find the house.
d) The neighbours complained about the noise.
questions.explanation: The text says: "In the end, his mother told him to find a proper workplace." The neighbours were his customers, not people who complained, and nothing is said about the university or customers getting lost.

questions.question: What do we learn about the money Josh borrowed?
options: a) He paid it back sooner than he had promised.
b) A bank lent it to him after several attempts.
c) His uncle later let him keep it as a gift.
d) He spent most of it on the rent for the shop.
questions.explanation: Josh "promised to pay it all back within two years. He managed it in eighteen months", so he paid it back early. The banks "did not want to lend money" to him, and the money was "for tools and spare parts", not for the rent.

questions.question: What does Josh think about his online repair videos?
options: a) They bring him customers in the end.
b) They take up too much of his free time.
c) They were a mistake in his first winter.
d) They have reduced the number of repairs he gets.
questions.explanation: Josh explains that when "something goes really wrong", viewers "remember my name. They trust me", so the videos bring him customers. Some customers fear he will "lose business", but Josh disagrees with them.

questions.question: What is the main advice Josh gives to other young people?
options: a) Keep a careful record of everything you buy.
b) Plan every detail before you start.
c) Find a partner with business experience.
d) Start now and learn from your mistakes.
questions.explanation: Josh says: "Don’t wait until you know everything" and "every mistake taught me something useful." Forgetting receipts is only one example of his mistakes, not his main advice, and planning every detail is the opposite of what he says.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 1?
questions.explanation: Biscuit had lived "alone in a small back garden", so a busy flat full of noise and visitors would be a shock; this explains why next "he hid behind the sofa". The sentence about him loving other dogs from the first day cannot fit, because it does not match a dog that hides and refuses to eat.
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 2?
questions.explanation: "This surprised us" refers back to "she did not bring any equipment", and the writers expected "a whistle or at least a lead". The sentence saying she arrived with a bag of toys and a lead is wrong, because the text says she brought no equipment.
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 3?
questions.explanation: "Before that" means before dogs "can learn anything", and "a regular routine helps" leads directly to "So we kept the same routine every day". No other sentence explains why the writers started a routine.
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 4?
questions.explanation: The lessons "never lasted more than five minutes", and this sentence gives the reason: "short, happy lessons work much better than long ones". The sentence saying cheese was the only food he would not eat is wrong, because the writers "used tiny pieces of cheese as rewards".
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Read the text "Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 5?
questions.explanation: "there" refers to "the park", and an "almost empty" park solves the problem that "Other dogs frightened him". The sentence saying he loved meeting other dogs contradicts "Other dogs frightened him".
options: A) Before that, they have to feel safe, and a regular routine helps with this.
B) Instead, she arrived with a large bag of toys and a long lead.
C) So for the first few months, we only took him there early in the morning, when it was almost empty.
D) So the noise and the visitors in our busy flat were a real shock to him.
E) Cheese was the only food that he would not eat.
F) Megan had told us that short, happy lessons work much better than long ones.
G) This surprised us, as we had expected a whistle or at least a lead.
H) That is why he loved meeting other dogs from the very first day.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: The text says "I had never spoken on the radio before". Speak can be used without an object; told, said and explained all need an object (told someone, said something, explained something), so they cannot fit here.
options: a) said
b) spoken
c) explained
d) told

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: Only advise follows the pattern verb + person + to-infinitive: "She advised me to start by reading the weather report". We cannot say suggested me to, insisted me to or proposed me to.
options: a) proposed
b) suggested
c) advised
d) insisted

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: The weather report "only lasted about two minutes": last means continue for a period of time. Spent needs a person as subject (I spent two minutes), passed needs time as subject, and kept does not describe how long something takes.
options: a) passed
b) kept
c) lasted
d) spent

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: At first the writer was "extremely nervous", but "after a couple of months" felt confident enough to ask for a programme. Being polite, careful or patient enough does not explain why the writer could now ask to present a show.
options: a) confident
b) polite
c) careful
d) patient

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: A radio presenter plays songs: "I play songs by new bands from our area". Put songs and turn songs are not correct English, and make songs would mean the writer writes the music.
options: a) put
b) turn
c) make
d) play

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: The structure is "has taught me how to plan my time": teach + person + how to. Learnt, studied and practised cannot be followed by a person (me) in this way.
options: a) learnt
b) studied
c) practised
d) taught

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: This is a past perfect passive: "The project had been planned for over a year". The project did not plan anything itself, so had must be followed by been + past participle.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: "Very few of us had ever planted a tree before, so a gardener … showed us what to do." The word so shows that most people had no experience; very many would not fit the meaning or the word ever.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: Tiring is a long adjective, so the comparative is more tiring than. "My back was aching" shows that the work was harder than expected, so less is not possible.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: The subject is the trees, so the reflexive pronoun is needed: "the trees are too young to look after themselves yet". Them would mean some other things, not the trees.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: Unless means if not: "They will not survive their first summer unless someone waters them regularly". If would give the opposite meaning (watering would kill them).

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: After a comma, a non-defining relative clause that refers to the whole idea before it starts with which: "organised a rota, which means that every volunteer …". That cannot be used after a comma.

questions.question:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Sophie and the notes you have made.

From: Sophie
Subject: A job at the café

Hi!
Guess what? The café where I work, Bean There, is looking for someone to help at weekends, and I immediately thought of you! [Note 1: Brilliant!] You’d work on Saturday and Sunday mornings from eight o’clock until one. Would those hours be OK for you? [Note 2: Explain] The work is mainly serving customers and clearing tables, but sometimes you’d help in the kitchen too. Which would you prefer to do? [Note 3: Tell Sophie] If you’re interested, my manager would like to meet you next week. When are you free? [Note 4: Suggest a day and time]

Love,
Sophie

Write your email to Sophie using all the notes. Write about 100 words.
questions.explanation:
A good answer replies to all four notes: (1) reacts with enthusiasm and thanks Sophie for thinking of you; (2) says whether the weekend hours are possible and explains why or why not; (3) says whether you prefer serving customers or working in the kitchen, and gives a reason; (4) suggests a day and a time to meet the manager. Use an informal greeting and ending, link your ideas (because, but, so) and write about 100 words.

Model answer:
Hi Sophie,
Thanks so much for thinking of me – that’s brilliant news! I’ve wanted a weekend job for ages.
Saturday mornings are perfect for me. On Sundays I have a swimming lesson at nine, so I couldn’t come before ten. Is that a problem?
I’d prefer to help in the kitchen because I love cooking and I’m a bit shy with new people. But I’m happy to serve customers too if you need me.
I could meet your manager next Tuesday or Wednesday after school, at about half past four. Would that be OK?
See you soon,
Alex

questions.question:
Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2 – Article
You see this announcement in an English-language magazine for young people.

Articles wanted!
MY FIRST JOB
What was your first job, or what job would you like to do first? What did you learn, or what would you like to learn? Was it what you expected?
Write an article answering these questions. We will publish the best articles in our magazine.

Write your article.

Question 3 – Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
It was my first day at work and I was late.

Write your story.
questions.explanation:
Article: give your article a title, answer all the questions in the announcement (what the job was or would be, what you learned or want to learn, whether it was as you expected) and try to interest the reader, for example with a question or a personal opinion. Story: begin with the given sentence, keep the same person and past tenses, and make sure the story has a clear middle and ending. In both tasks write about 100 words and link your ideas clearly.

Model article:
My first job
Last summer I got my first job at a garden centre near my home. I watered the plants, helped customers carry heavy bags to their cars and kept the shop tidy.
I learned a lot. I learned how to talk politely to people I didn’t know, and how to work in a team. I also discovered that I’m good at remembering the names of flowers!
Was it what I expected? Not really. I thought it would be easy, but I was on my feet all day and I felt really tired in the evenings. Still, I loved earning my own money.

Model story:
It was my first day at work and I was late. My bus had broken down, so I ran the last kilometre to the bookshop. When I arrived, the door was closed and there was nobody inside. I waited outside, feeling terrible.
Ten minutes later, the owner, Mrs Hill, arrived with a bag of keys. “I’m so sorry,” she said. “My alarm didn’t ring this morning!”
We both started laughing. She made us some tea and showed me how everything worked. By lunchtime I felt completely relaxed, and I knew I was going to enjoy working there.

questions.question:
Part 1 – Interview
The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question and give some extra information.

Where do you live?
Can you tell us something about your home?
Which room in your home do you like best? Why?
What do you like about your neighbourhood?
Is there anything you would like to change about the area where you live?
questions.explanation:
Give full answers, not just one or two words: answer the question, then add a reason or an example. Use present tenses for your daily life and would for things you want to change.

Model answers:
I live in a flat in the north of the city, quite close to the river.
It’s not very big, but it’s comfortable. There are three bedrooms and a small balcony where we have some plants.
I like my bedroom best, because it’s quiet and I can listen to music or read there without anyone disturbing me.
The best thing is that everything is near. There’s a supermarket, a park and a bus stop just round the corner.
I’d like to have a swimming pool nearby. At the moment I have to take two buses to go swimming, which takes ages.

questions.question:
Part 2 – Photo description
Look at the photograph. It shows a family doing jobs together in a kitchen. An adult is washing dishes at the sink, a teenager is drying plates with a towel and a young child is putting knives and forks into a drawer. A dog is sitting on the floor next to the child. The kitchen is bright, and there is a bowl of fruit on the table. Everyone is smiling. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.

Talk for about one minute.
questions.explanation:
Describe the place, the people and what each person is doing, using the present continuous (is washing, is drying). Say where things are (next to, on the table, at the sink). If you do not know a word, explain it in other words. You can give your opinion about the people, but only from what you can see.

Model answer:
In this photo I can see a family in their kitchen. They’re all doing jobs together. First, an adult is washing the dishes at the sink. A teenager is drying the plates with a towel. There’s also a young child, who is putting knives and forks into a drawer. I can see a dog too – it’s sitting on the floor next to the child. The kitchen looks bright, and there’s a bowl of fruit on the table. Everyone is smiling, so I think they don’t mind helping. It looks like they enjoy working together.

questions.question:
Part 3 – Collaborative task
The local council wants to make a neighbourhood a better place for young people. Here are some ideas they are thinking about.

a skate park
a youth club with games and music
a free outdoor cinema in summer
more cycle paths
a community garden
free sports lessons at weekends

Talk together about how each idea could help young people in the neighbourhood. Then decide which idea would be the best.

Talk together for about two or three minutes.
questions.explanation:
Talk about the ideas one by one and give reasons. Ask your partner for their opinion, agree and disagree politely, and try to reach a decision together at the end. Useful language: What do you think about …? I agree, but … That’s a good point. Shall we choose …?

Model conversation (part):
A: Shall we start with the skate park? I think lots of teenagers would use it.
B: Yes, but not everyone likes skateboarding. A youth club would be good for more people, because there are games and music.
A: That’s true. And it’s open in winter too, when it’s cold and dark. What about the cycle paths?
B: They’re useful and safer, but they’re not really a place to meet friends.
A: I agree. So the youth club or the free sports lessons?
B: I’d say the youth club, because it’s for everyone, even people who don’t like sport.
A: OK, let’s choose the youth club.

questions.question:
Part 4 – General conversation
The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about homes and neighbours. Give your opinion and talk to your partner too.

Do you know your neighbours well? Why or why not?
How can neighbours help each other?
Is it better to live in a city or in the countryside? Why?
What do young people in your area do in their free time?
What kind of home would you like to live in in the future?
questions.explanation:
Give your opinion with a reason or an example, and react to what your partner says (I agree with you, but …; That’s interesting – in my town …). Use would for the future question.

Model answers:
I know some of my neighbours quite well. The woman next door looks after our cat when we go on holiday, and we water her plants in return.
Neighbours can help by carrying shopping for older people, or by keeping an eye on a house when the family is away.
Personally, I prefer the city, because there’s more to do and better public transport. But the countryside is quieter and the air is cleaner.
In my area, young people mostly meet in the park or go to the shopping centre. Some play football at the sports ground.
In the future I’d like to live in a small house with a garden, maybe near the sea.

questions.question: What did the woman see on her walk?
options: a) a deer
b) a fox
c) some rabbits
questions.explanation: The woman says "guess what I saw by the river? A deer!" The man is the one who has seen foxes, and she says there were no rabbits: "there weren’t any today".

questions.question: Where is the cat now?
options: a) on the garage roof
b) inside the garage
c) under the bed
questions.explanation: The noise is "coming from inside the garage" and the woman finds him "next to the bikes". He was on the roof earlier, but "He isn’t there now", and she has already looked under the bed.

questions.question: What does the woman tell the man to do?
options: a) give the dog less food
b) walk the dog for longer
c) buy a different dog food
questions.explanation: The woman says "The problem is exercise" and tells him to "make each walk at least forty minutes". She says "his food is fine" and he is "eating the right amount", so he should not change it or give less.

questions.question: Which animals will the woman photograph for the competition?
options: a) the lions
b) the penguins
c) the giraffes
questions.explanation: When the man suggests the giraffes, she answers "Yes, they’re the ones". She does not want the lions because "Everyone will take pictures" of them, and the penguins are "behind glass".

questions.question: How many puppies did Bella have?
options: a) eight
b) five
c) six
questions.explanation: The woman says "in the end there were five". Eight is the number the vet expected, and six is the number of people who have "asked us for one".

questions.question: What will the man do at the animal centre this Saturday?
options: a) clean the cages
b) feed the rabbits
c) walk some dogs
questions.explanation: The man says "this Saturday they’ve asked me to take some of the dogs out for walks". He fed the rabbits "Last week", and they already have "enough people" for cleaning the cages.

questions.question: What will the children do first at the farm?
options: a) feed the goats
b) visit the lambs
c) ride the ponies
questions.explanation: The woman says "let’s start by giving the goats some food". The ponies are for two o’clock, and the lambs come "after the ponies".

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a new café. What does the woman think of it?
options: a) It costs too much to go there often.
b) She is still sad that the bookshop closed.
c) It keeps something of the old shop.
questions.explanation: She says "They’ve kept some of the old shelves" and "It feels like the bookshop never really left". She was sad when the bookshop closed, "But the café’s lovely", and about the price she says "I don’t mind".

questions.question: You will hear two neighbours talking about a plan to close a road to cars. What do they agree about?
options: a) Local people should be asked first.
b) The shops will lose customers.
c) The plan will be good for children.
questions.explanation: The man says "the council should ask the people who live here before it decides anything" and the woman replies "Absolutely". They disagree about the shops ("I think they’ll get more people walking past"), and the woman is "not sure many children would use it".

questions.question: You will hear a woman telling a friend about a street party she organised. How does she feel about it now?
options: a) Disappointed that so few people came
b) Glad that she made the effort
c) Worried about how much it cost
questions.explanation: It was "hard work" and she "nearly gave up twice", but she says "I’m really glad I did it" and will do it again. About "sixty people came", and it "hardly cost anything" because the council lent the tables.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a local meeting. Why is the man going to it?
options: a) To ask about parking problems
b) To complain about the building work
c) To support a plan for a playground
questions.explanation: He says the council wants to build a playground and "I want to speak up for it". He expects other people to "complain about parking", and the building work is the woman’s problem; he says it will "be finished in a month".

questions.question: You will hear a woman talking to a friend about her new flat. What does she like most about the area?
options: a) It is close to where she works.
b) Her neighbours are very kind.
c) It is next to a busy main road.
questions.explanation: About the neighbours she says "That’s the best thing": one brought her a cake and another helped carry her sofa. Being near the main road worried her at first, and work is "Twenty minutes on the bus", the same as before.

questions.question: You will hear two friends talking about a piece of local news. What is the man’s opinion of the plan for the old cinema?
options: a) It is sensible, although it is a pity.
b) It will make the town centre too busy.
c) The cinema should be repaired instead.
questions.explanation: He says "It’s sad" but "flats make sense" because young people "can’t find anywhere to live". Repairing the cinema is what other people want; he asks "who would go?". He never talks about the town centre being busy.

questions.question: This year, writers must be aged between 11 and ____.
questions.explanation: Eighteen was last year’s limit. This year: "if you’re aged between eleven and sixteen, you can take part".

questions.question: Subject of this year’s stories: a ____
questions.explanation: "This year we want you to write a story about a journey." Friendship was the subject of "last year’s stories".

questions.question: Maximum length of the story: ____ words
questions.explanation: "Your story mustn’t be longer than eight hundred words." Five hundred is the limit in "some competitions", not this one.

questions.question: The three best stories will be read on the radio by a famous ____.
questions.explanation: The stories will be read "not by me … but by a well-known actor". The presenter will not read them.

questions.question: Prize for the winner: a ____
