Rhys joined eight years ago, after he got lost himself. 'I'd gone up a mountain in trainers, without a map, and the cloud came down,' he remembers, smiling. 'I'm embarrassed about it now. The team found me in about an hour, and they didn't make me feel stupid at all. I decided I wanted to do the same for other people.'

Becoming a member wasn't quick. New volunteers train for about a year before they go out on real rescues, learning first aid, how to use ropes and how to find their way at night. Rhys admits he nearly gave up. 'I thought I was fit, but carrying a heavy stretcher down a steep hill in the rain is something else. I was always the slowest.' What kept him going, he says, was the support of the older members, who never criticised him.

The team is called out more than a hundred times a year, and the number is growing. Rhys believes social media is partly responsible. 'Someone posts a beautiful photo from the top of a mountain, and thousands of people want to go there. Many of them have no idea how quickly the weather can change.' However, he doesn't want people to stay away. 'We'd much rather people came well prepared, with warm clothes, a map and a charged phone, than not at all.'

That October night, the walker turned out to have a broken ankle. It took the team four hours to carry her down. Rhys got home after two in the morning and opened his shop as usual at nine. Is it worth it? 'Every time,' he says.

passages.title: Our year without plastic
passages.text:
When Sophie Marsh emptied her kitchen bin one evening in January, she counted the plastic inside: fourteen bags, nine food trays and a broken toy. 'That was just two days' rubbish for a family of four,' she says. (1) ________ Their two children, aged eight and eleven, were much less enthusiastic.

The first weeks were the hardest. Almost everything in their usual supermarket came wrapped in plastic, from cucumbers to cheese. (2) ________ Some of the stallholders found this strange at first, but most were happy to help.

Food was not the only problem. Shampoo, toothpaste and washing-up liquid all came in plastic bottles. (3) ________ Her homemade toothpaste, she admits, was not a success. 'It tasted like salty chalk,' laughs her son, Leo.

Living without plastic also took a lot of time. Dan worked out that the family spent about four extra hours a week shopping and cooking. (4) ________ By the end of the year, their food bills had fallen by almost a fifth.

The experiment ended last December. The family did not manage to avoid plastic completely, because some things, such as medicines, were impossible to buy without it. But their rubbish fell from two full bins a week to one small bag a month. (5) ________ Leo, who complained the most at the beginning, now gives talks about it at his school.

passages.title: From brick to smartphone
passages.text:
Today almost everyone carries a mobile phone, but the first ones looked very different. In 1983, one of the earliest mobile phones (1) ____ on sale in the United States. It weighed nearly a kilogram, its battery lasted for (2) ____ thirty minutes, and it cost almost four thousand dollars.

During the 1990s, phones became smaller and cheaper, and people started sending text messages. At first, each message could only (3) ____ up to 160 characters, so users invented short forms like "CU L8R" for "see you later".

The biggest change came in 2007, when smartphones with large touch screens became popular. Suddenly people could take photos, listen to music and search the internet without (4) ____ a computer. Within a few years, these phones had (5) ____ the place of cameras, maps and even alarm clocks for millions of people.

Some experts are worried that we now spend too much time looking at our screens. However, it is hard to (6) ____ life without these clever little machines, and they will probably continue to change in ways we cannot yet predict.

passages.title: Where was Biscuit?
passages.text:
Last winter our cat, Biscuit, disappeared. He always comes home for his dinner at six o'clock, so when he didn't appear, we started to worry.

We searched the garden and the street with torches, but by midnight we (1) ____ still not found him anywhere. The next day my sister made posters with his photo, and we put them on every lamp post in the neighbourhood. Several people called, but none of the cats they had seen was Biscuit.

By Thursday, Biscuit had been missing (2) ____ Sunday evening, and we were starting to give (3) ____ hope. Then, at ten o'clock that night, our neighbour Mr Davies knocked on the door. He had been clearing out his garage and had heard a quiet noise behind some old paint tins.

I ran next door as fast (4) ____ I could. There was Biscuit, dusty and (5) ____ thin that I hardly recognised him. He must have walked into the garage while the door was open and got trapped.

It wasn't (6) ____ he had eaten two bowls of food that he finally began to purr. Now we always check Mr Davies's garage first!

passages.title: Recording 1
passages.text:
Man: Have you got anything for your brother’s birthday yet? Oliver’s going to be sixteen, isn’t he?
Woman: Yes, and I’ve finally found something. I was going to get him a shirt for his football team, but they didn’t have his size.
Man: What about that board game he keeps talking about?
Woman: Mum’s already bought him that. So in the end I got him some headphones. His old ones are broken.
Man: Good idea. He’ll use them every day.

passages.title: Recording 2
passages.text:
Woman: Are you going to Rachel’s leaving party at the office tomorrow?
Man: Yes, and I still haven’t got her anything. I thought about flowers, but they’ll be dead in a week.
Woman: She loves cooking, doesn’t she? What about a recipe book?
Man: She’s got hundreds of those. No, I know. She’s always saying her desk looks empty, so I’ll get her a little plant for her new office.
Woman: Perfect. She’ll love that.

passages.title: Recording 3
passages.text:
Woman: Look, I’ve bought this scarf for my aunt.
Man: It’s lovely. Was it expensive?
Woman: Well, the label said thirty pounds, but there was a sale on, so it was twenty-four. And then the shop assistant noticed a small mark on it and took another six pounds off.
Man: So you paid eighteen pounds? That’s a good price. I can hardly see the mark.

passages.title: Recording 4
passages.text:
Man: I’ve decided what to give my mum and dad for their wedding anniversary. I’m taking them out for a meal at that new Italian restaurant.
Woman: How lovely! The anniversary’s on Friday, isn’t it?
Man: Yes, but Dad doesn’t finish work until nine on Fridays. I wanted to go on Saturday evening instead, but the restaurant was fully booked. So we’re going for lunch on Sunday.
Woman: That sounds perfect.

passages.title: Recording 5
passages.text:
Woman: Granny’s eightieth birthday is next month. What shall we give her?
Man: You’re good at baking. Why don’t you make her a cake?
Woman: Auntie Sue’s already making one. We could make her a birthday card, I suppose.
Man: She’ll get lots of cards. What about putting some old family photos into an album?
Woman: Oh yes, she’d love that. Let’s start looking for photos this weekend.

passages.title: Recording 6
passages.text:
Woman: I can’t decide which bag to get for Lucy. This striped one is fun.
Man: Hmm, but she isn’t really a beach person, is she? What about the black backpack? She cycles to work.
Woman: She’s just bought one, actually. No, I think she’d like the brown leather one best. It goes with everything.
Man: It’s more expensive, though.
Woman: That’s fine. She’s my best friend.

passages.title: Recording 7
passages.text: Woman: Good afternoon, shoppers. If you’re looking for that special present, don’t forget our gift-wrapping service on the ground floor. Our normal closing time is half past five, but this week, to help with your Christmas shopping, the store is staying open until seven o’clock. Please note that the gift-wrapping desk closes earlier, at six. Thank you for shopping with us.

passages.title: Dialogue 1
passages.text:
Woman: Are you still using that running app?
Man: Every day! I know it isn’t free, and it took me a few days to understand all the buttons, but now it’s easy. Honestly, without it I’d have stopped running weeks ago. When it tells me I’ve beaten my best time, I just want to go out again the next morning.
Woman: Maybe I should try it, then.
Man: You should. It’s worth every penny.

passages.title: Dialogue 2
passages.text:
Woman: I had my first video call with Grandma and Grandad last night.
Man: How did it go? I bet it took ages to get them connected.
Woman: That’s what I expected! I was ready to spend an hour explaining which buttons to press. But Grandad had practised with a neighbour, and it worked first time. We chatted for ages, and I could hear them perfectly.
Man: That’s brilliant.
Woman: Honestly, it was the best part of my week.

passages.title: Dialogue 3
passages.text:
Man: How are you getting on with the new booking system?
Woman: Not very well! I’m sure it’s better than the old one, but nobody showed us how it works.
Man: Exactly. We had one short email from the manager and that was it. They should have given us a proper course before it started.
Woman: I agree. I spent half the morning asking people for help.
Man: Me too. Maybe it’ll save us time when we know what we’re doing, but I’m not so sure.

passages.title: Dialogue 4
passages.text:
Man: Are you still learning Spanish with that app?
Woman: No, I gave up last month.
Man: Really? I thought it was free.
Woman: It is, and the games were fun. I learned loads of words. But when I went to Valencia, I couldn’t have a single conversation with anyone. All I’d done was press buttons! So now I go to an evening class where we actually talk to each other.
Man: That sounds much more useful.

passages.title: Dialogue 5
passages.text:
Man: So did your family really spend a whole evening without phones?
Woman: We did. To be honest, I thought I’d hate it. I thought I’d keep worrying about missing messages.
Man: And did you?
Woman: For about ten minutes! Then we got a board game out and laughed all evening. My kids didn’t even ask for their phones. We’re going to do it every Friday now.

passages.title: Dialogue 6
passages.text:
Woman: Nice watch! Is that one of those smart watches?
Man: Yes. Everyone thinks I got it for my messages, but my phone’s fine for that.
Woman: So is it for running?
Man: Not really. The doctor said I wasn’t sleeping enough, so I wanted to know how many hours I really get each night. The watch shows me every morning. It’s already made me go to bed earlier.
Woman: And it looks good too.
Man: That’s just a bonus.

passages.title: A tour of the Kingsley Theatre
passages.text:
Woman: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Kingsley Theatre. My name’s Helen and I’ll be your guide this morning. The tour takes about an hour, so I hope you’re all wearing comfortable shoes.

Let’s start with a bit of history. A lot of visitors think this building was once a church, because of the tall windows, but in fact it was built as a fish market. It only became a theatre in 1904, when a local businessman bought it and turned it into the place you see today.

Now, if you follow me into the main hall… Here we are. When the theatre first opened, it had space for twelve hundred people, but in those days the seats were very narrow. After we put in new, more comfortable seats ten years ago, the number went down, and today we have eight hundred and fifty seats.

Do look up at the ceiling. People usually expect a theatre ceiling to be red, but ours is green, with little gold stars painted all over it. It was cleaned last spring, so the colours are really bright again.

Next we’re going backstage. Down these stairs is the workshop where the costumes are made. We have a team of four people who make everything by hand. The wigs, by the way, aren’t made here. We order those from a company in London.

Right, now we’re on the stage itself. You’re welcome to walk around, and you can even sit on the furniture, which is from tonight’s show. The only thing I must ask is that you don’t touch the ropes at the side of the stage. They hold up the scenery, and they’re very heavy.

That’s nearly the end of the tour. Before you go, keep hold of your ticket. If you show it in the café on the ground floor, you’ll get ten per cent off anything you buy there today. I’m afraid the discount doesn’t work in the gift shop, though. Thank you all for coming, and I hope you enjoy the rest of your day.

passages.title: Interview with a baker
passages.text:
Interviewer: Today I’m talking to Megan Price, who opened her own bakery in the town of Ludlow two years ago. Megan, you used to work in an office, didn’t you?

Megan: That’s right, I was in a bank for six years. The pay was fine and my colleagues were lovely, so people were surprised when I left. But I’d been baking at weekends for years, and I realised that Saturday mornings in the kitchen were the only time I felt really happy. In the end, I just couldn’t keep doing a job I didn’t care about.

Interviewer: How did you feel on the day the shop opened?

Megan: Honestly, I was terrified. Not about the baking, because I knew my bread was good. I kept thinking: what if I’ve spent all my savings and nobody comes through the door? Then at half past seven there was a queue outside, and I nearly cried.

Interviewer: Bakers start work very early. How do you cope with that?

Megan: I start at four. Everyone warned me it would be awful, but actually I don’t mind it at all. The streets are quiet, the radio’s on, and I get more done in those two hours than I used to in a whole day at the bank. What I do find hard is going to bed at nine.

Interviewer: What makes a good bakery, in your opinion?

Megan: Lots of people would say the recipes, and of course they matter. But for me, it’s the people behind the counter. If customers feel welcome, if you remember their names and what they like, they’ll come back even on a day when the croissants aren’t perfect.

Interviewer: A lot of people buy their bread in supermarkets. Does that worry you?

Megan: Not really. Some supermarket bread is perfectly nice, and it’s cheaper than mine, I know that. But I don’t think we’re really competing. People come to me for a treat, or for something special at the weekend, not for their everyday sandwich loaf.

Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to young people who’d like to start their own business?

Megan: Don’t wait until everything is perfect, because it never will be. But do get some experience first. I worked in another baker’s shop on Saturdays for a year before I opened mine, and I learned more there than from any book.

Interviewer: Megan Price, thank you very much.

passages.title: Riverside Recycling Centre
passages.text: Glass bottles and jars go in the green containers. Please remove the lids first. From 1 March, we can no longer accept window glass or mirrors – please take these to the general waste area next to the car park.

passages.title: Text message
passages.text: Hi Tom, the beach clean-up on Saturday starts at 9, not 10 as it says on the poster. Gloves and rubbish bags are provided, but bring your own water – there’s no café nearby. See you there! Priya

passages.title: Sign on a bin
passages.text: PAPER AND CARD ONLY. Please flatten all boxes before you put them in. Pizza boxes with food on them cannot be recycled and should go in the black bin instead.

passages.title: Greenfield Town Clean-Up – Sunday 14 April
passages.text: Volunteers meet outside the library at 10 am. Children under 12 are welcome but must come with an adult. There’s a free lunch for everyone who helps! Please sign up online by Thursday so that we can order enough food.

passages.title: Email from Westbury Council Waste Team
passages.text: Because of the bank holiday on Monday, all bin collections next week will be one day later than usual. Garden waste will not be collected at all next week. Normal collections start again the week after.

passages.title: A – Clifftop Sunrise Walk
passages.text: This 6 km coastal path along the Pembrokeshire cliffs is at its best at dawn, when the early light turns the rocks gold and the sea shines below you. Set off early and you’ll probably have the path to yourself – by mid-morning in summer it gets very busy. There are some steep steps down to a small beach.

passages.title: B – Woodland and Waterfall Walk
passages.text: A short walk of just under an hour through ancient oak woods to Pistyll Falls. The path climbs steeply in places, and there are 120 steps up to the viewing platform, but the view of the water crashing down is worth the effort. The café at the car park makes a good place to rest afterwards.

passages.title: C – Heron Marsh Nature Reserve
passages.text: The number 42 bus stops right at the entrance to this reserve. Easy wooden paths lead to hides where you can watch herons, otters and, in spring, hundreds of ducklings. Dogs on leads are welcome on all paths. Children can pick up a free spotter’s sheet at the visitor centre and tick off everything they see.

passages.title: D – Castle Bay Promenade
passages.text: This wide, level path follows the seafront for 3 km to Penrhos Castle, built in the thirteenth century. The surface is smooth all the way, so it suits wheelchairs and pushchairs, and boards along the route tell the story of the castle and its battles. It’s one of the busiest paths in the area, especially on sunny afternoons.

passages.title: E – Three Tops Challenge
passages.text: A tough 25 km route over three mountain summits, with amazing views of the lakes and the coast from each one. Allow at least nine hours. There are no signs along the way and the paths are hard to follow in cloud, so you must be able to use a map and compass. Only for experienced walkers.

passages.title: F – Riverside Mill Trail
passages.text: A gentle 4 km loop along the River Usk which is completely flat and takes around an hour and a half. It finishes at the old mill, now a tea room serving light lunches and homemade cakes. There are benches every few hundred metres, which makes it ideal for anyone who likes to take regular breaks.

passages.title: G – Plas Hendre Deer Park
passages.text: Walk through the grounds of a seventeenth-century country house, where herds of red deer wander freely. The station is only ten minutes away on foot. The grass paths are uneven and often muddy, so they are not suitable for wheelchairs. Please note that dogs are not allowed in the park, as they frighten the deer.

passages.title: H – Cadair Summit Day
passages.text: Join one of our experienced guides for a seven-hour climb to the top of Cadair Idris, 893 metres high. On a clear day you can see all the way to Ireland from the summit. Good fitness and proper boots are essential. Groups of up to ten leave the visitor centre every Saturday at 8 am.

passages.title: The teenager who fixes the city’s bikes
passages.text:
Josh Turner was nineteen when he opened his bicycle repair shop in Leeds. Three years later, the little shop near the canal is busy every day. However, the beginning was not easy.

Josh has loved bikes all his life. His grandfather taught him to mend punctures in the garden shed. “I spent every weekend with oily hands,” he says. At school he was not interested in most subjects, because he preferred taking things apart and putting them back together. After school he started an engineering course at college, but he left after one year. “The course was mostly theory. I wanted to work with real machines,” he explains.

For the next year he repaired bikes for friends and neighbours in his parents’ garage. He charged very little, so soon strangers were knocking on the door with broken bikes. His parents were patient, but the garage was always full. In the end, his mother told him to find a proper workplace.

Josh found an empty shop with a cheap rent, but the problem was money. The banks did not want to lend money to a teenager with no business experience. Finally, his uncle lent him £4,000 for tools and spare parts. Josh promised to pay it all back within two years. He managed it in eighteen months.

The first winter was hard because few people cycle in cold, wet weather, and customers were rare. Some weeks Josh earned almost nothing. He used the quiet time well, though, and built a simple website and started posting short repair videos. In them he shows easy jobs, like adjusting gears or cleaning a chain. Some customers were surprised. “Why do you teach people to fix their own bikes? You’ll lose business!” they said. Josh disagrees. “People watch the videos and try the job at home. Sometimes something goes really wrong. Then they remember my name. They trust me, because I’ve already helped them for free.”

Today Josh employs two part-time mechanics, both students. He also runs a free repair class for local children every Saturday morning. “Lots of kids have bikes with flat tyres in the garage. Nobody shows them how to fix them,” he says.

What advice would he give to other young people? “Don’t wait until you know everything. I made plenty of mistakes in my first year. I ordered the wrong parts, and I forgot to keep receipts. But every mistake taught me something useful.” He smiles. “And find an uncle with some savings!”

passages.title: Learning to trust: a year with Biscuit
passages.text:
Last spring, my partner and I adopted a three-year-old dog called Biscuit from a rescue centre near Leeds. The staff told us that he had spent most of his life alone in a small back garden. (1) ________ For the first two days, he hid behind the sofa and refused to eat anything at all.

In the end, we contacted a local trainer called Megan Hughes. On her first visit, she did not bring any equipment with her. (2) ________ For an hour, she simply sat on the floor with a book and completely ignored Biscuit. By the end of that hour, he was lying next to her feet.

Megan explained that many rescue dogs need time before they can learn anything. (3) ________ So we kept the same routine every day: a walk at seven, breakfast at eight and a quiet hour in the afternoon. After about three weeks, Biscuit started to relax.

Then the real training began. We used tiny pieces of cheese as rewards, and the lessons never lasted more than five minutes. (4) ________ Biscuit learned to sit in a single afternoon, but learning to stay took him much longer.

The hardest part was the park. Other dogs frightened him, and he barked at every bicycle. (5) ________ Now, a year later, he can walk past a busy playground without even looking up. He still hides behind the sofa sometimes, but these days it is usually because he has stolen a sock.

passages.title: On air at college
passages.text: When I started college last year, a friend persuaded me to join the student radio station. I had never (1) ______ on the radio before, so I was extremely nervous at my first meeting. Luckily, the station manager, Priya, was very kind. She (2) ______ me to start by reading the weather report, which only (3) ______ about two minutes. Even so, my hands were shaking the first time the red light came on. Little by little, it got easier. After a couple of months I felt (4) ______ enough to ask for my own music programme, and Priya agreed. Now, every Thursday evening from eight to nine, I (5) ______ songs by new bands from our area and chat about them with guests. Some listeners even send messages to request their favourite tracks. Working at the station has (6) ______ me how to plan my time and how to work as part of a team. Next term I am hoping to interview a few local musicians live in the studio, which will be my biggest challenge so far.

passages.title: Five hundred new trees
passages.text: Last autumn our town council asked local people to help plant five hundred young trees along the river path. The project had (1) ______ planned for over a year, but the money only arrived in the summer. On a cold Saturday morning about sixty volunteers met at the old bridge, carrying spades and flasks of hot tea. Very (2) ______ of us had ever planted a tree before, so a gardener from the council showed us what to do. By lunchtime my back was aching, and the work was far (3) ______ tiring than I had expected. Still, it felt good to see the long line of thin trees standing in the grass. The gardener explained that the trees are too young to look after (4) ______ yet. They will not survive their first summer (5) ______ someone waters them regularly. The council has now organised a rota, (6) ______ means that every volunteer spends one evening a month with a watering can. My turn is next Tuesday, and I am already looking forward to it.

passages.title: Recording 1
passages.text:
Man: You’re back early from your walk.
Woman: It started raining. But guess what I saw by the river? A deer! It was just standing there, drinking.
Man: Really? I’ve only ever seen foxes round here.
Woman: I usually see rabbits in the field next to the river, but there weren’t any today. The deer ran off as soon as it heard me.

passages.title: Recording 2
passages.text:
Woman: Have you seen Tiger? I’ve looked under the bed and in all the cupboards.
Man: He was on the garage roof earlier, sitting in the sun.
Woman: He isn’t there now. I’ve just looked.
Man: Wait, listen. Can you hear that? It’s coming from inside the garage. I left the door open when I got the bikes out. He must have gone in there.
Woman: Oh yes, there he is, next to the bikes. Silly cat!

passages.title: Recording 3
passages.text:
Woman: Well, I’ve checked Max all over. He’s healthy, but he’s a bit heavy for a dog of his size.
Man: Oh dear. Should I change his food, or give him less?
Woman: No, his food is fine, and he’s eating the right amount. The problem is exercise. How long are his walks?
Man: About fifteen minutes, twice a day.
Woman: That isn’t enough for a young dog like Max. Try to make each walk at least forty minutes, and bring him back to see me in a month.

passages.title: Recording 4
passages.text:
Man: So which animal are you going to photograph for the competition?
Woman: Everyone will take pictures of the lions, so I don’t want to do that. I thought about the penguins, but they’re inside, behind glass, and you get terrible reflections.
Man: What about the giraffes? They’re outside, and the light’s lovely there in the afternoon.
Woman: Yes, they’re the ones. I’ll go over there after lunch.

passages.title: Recording 5
passages.text:
Woman: Did you hear? Our dog Bella had her puppies last night.
Man: Oh, that’s exciting! How many?
Woman: The vet thought there would be eight, but in the end there were five.
Man: Are you going to keep them all?
Woman: No way! Six people have already asked us for one, so finding homes for them won’t be a problem.

passages.title: Recording 6
passages.text:
Man: I’ve started volunteering at the animal centre on Saturdays.
Woman: Really? What do you do there? Clean the cages?
Man: Most volunteers do that, but they’ve got enough people for it now. Last week I fed the rabbits, but this Saturday they’ve asked me to take some of the dogs out for walks.
Woman: That sounds like the best job of all.

passages.title: Recording 7
passages.text: Woman: Welcome to Hill Farm, boys and girls. Now, I know you all want to ride the ponies, but they’re having a rest at the moment, so we’ll do that at two o’clock. The baby lambs are asleep in the barn, so we’ll visit them after the ponies. So let’s start by giving the goats some food. Take a bag each from the box by the gate, and follow me.

passages.title: Dialogue 1
passages.text:
Man: Have you been to the new café where the bookshop used to be?
Woman: Yes, I went on Saturday. I was sad when the bookshop closed, I must admit. But the café’s lovely. They’ve kept some of the old shelves, and there are books you can borrow while you have your coffee.
Man: Isn’t it expensive, though?
Woman: A bit more than the place by the station, but I don’t mind. It feels like the bookshop never really left.

passages.title: Dialogue 2
passages.text:
Woman: Did you read in the local paper that the council wants to close Mill Road to cars on Sunday mornings?
Man: I did. The idea is that children can play in the street.
Woman: I’m not sure many children would use it, actually. And the shopkeepers are worried they’ll lose customers.
Man: I think they’ll get more people walking past. But the council should ask the people who live here before it decides anything.
Woman: Absolutely. Nobody’s asked us a thing.

passages.title: Dialogue 3
passages.text:
Man: How was the street party in the end?
Woman: Well, it was hard work. Weeks of letters, phone calls, borrowing tables. I nearly gave up twice.
Man: Was it expensive?
Woman: No, the council lent us the tables for free, so it hardly cost anything. And on the day about sixty people came. I talked to neighbours I’d never spoken to in ten years of living there.
Man: So will you do it again next year?
Woman: Definitely. I’m really glad I did it.

passages.title: Dialogue 4
passages.text:
Woman: Are you going to the meeting at the library tonight?
Man: Yes. I expect most people will complain about parking.
Woman: It’s the building work that bothers me. It’s so noisy.
Man: That’ll be finished in a month. No, I’m going because they want to turn the empty land behind the school into a playground, and some people are against it. My kids have got nowhere to play round here, so I want to speak up for it.
Woman: Good for you.

passages.title: Dialogue 5
passages.text:
Man: How’s the new flat in Ashford Street?
Woman: I love it. I was worried because it’s near the main road, but my bedroom’s at the back, so I hardly hear the traffic.
Man: And the neighbours?
Woman: That’s the best thing. The day I moved in, the woman next door brought me a cake, and the man upstairs helped me carry my sofa. In my old street nobody even said hello.
Man: Is it far from work?
Woman: Twenty minutes on the bus. About the same as before.

passages.title: Dialogue 6
passages.text:
Woman: Did you see in the paper that the Regal Cinema is going to be turned into flats?
Man: Yes. It’s sad. I saw my first film there.
Woman: Lots of people are saying the council should repair it and open it again.
Man: I’d love that, but who would go? It’s been closed for eight years, and everyone watches films at the big cinema by the shopping centre now. Young people round here can’t find anywhere to live, so flats make sense.
Woman: I suppose you’re right.

passages.title: Radio Harbourside Young Writers’ Competition
passages.text:
Man: And now some exciting news for all you young writers out there. Here at Radio Harbourside we’re running our Young Writers’ Competition again, and this year it’s bigger than ever.

First of all, who can enter? Last year the competition was open to anyone between eleven and eighteen, but we had so many entries from older teenagers that this year we’re making it just for younger writers. So, if you’re aged between eleven and sixteen, you can take part.

Now, the subject. Last year’s stories were all about friendship, and we read some wonderful ones. This year we want you to write a story about a journey. It could be a trip to the other side of the world or just the walk to school. Use your imagination!

Your story mustn’t be longer than eight hundred words. I know some competitions ask for five hundred, but we want to give you a bit more space. Please don’t go over the limit, though, or the judges won’t read it.

Here’s the really exciting part. The three best stories will be read out on the radio in June. Not by me, I’m pleased to say, but by a well-known actor. We can’t tell you who yet, but you’ll certainly recognise the voice.

And the prizes? Everyone on the shortlist gets a set of books, and the winner will receive a laptop, which we hope will help with all your future writing.

To enter, just send your story to the address on our website before the thirtieth of April. Don’t forget to put your name and age at the top. We won’t be sending emails to tell people the results. Instead, the winners will be contacted by phone in the middle of May, so make sure you include a phone number for a parent or carer.

Good luck, everybody. We can’t wait to read your stories.

passages.title: Interview with a young business owner
passages.text:
Interviewer: My guest today is Aisha Bello, who’s just twenty-three and runs her own recycling business in Leeds. Aisha, tell us what you do.

Aisha: We collect old jeans from charity shops, from people’s wardrobes, from anywhere really, and turn them into bags, cushions and pencil cases. Last year we saved about four tonnes of denim from going to the rubbish tip.

Interviewer: How did the idea start?

Aisha: At university I shared a flat with three other students, and when we moved out, the amount of clothing we threw away shocked me. I’d always thought of myself as someone who cared about the environment, and suddenly I felt quite ashamed. That’s really what got me started. Making money didn’t come into it at first.

Interviewer: Was it difficult to get going?

Aisha: The sewing wasn’t a problem. My grandmother taught me when I was small. The hard part was persuading shops to stock our products. Some of them said recycled things looked cheap. I had to keep going back with better and better samples, and eventually one shop in York said yes.

Interviewer: You now have six people working for you. What’s that like?

Aisha: I love it, although being a boss was a big change. At first I tried to check everything myself, and I was exhausted. Now I trust the team to make their own decisions, and honestly, they often have better ideas than I do.

Interviewer: Your bags aren’t cheap, are they?

Aisha: No, and I won’t pretend they are. Every one is made by hand here in Leeds, and we pay our staff properly. Some customers do complain, but most of them understand that if you want something made fairly, it’s going to cost a bit more.

Interviewer: Some people say small recycling businesses can’t really make a difference. What do you think?

Aisha: I understand why they say it. One small company won’t save the planet. But I think we do something important by showing people that old things can be beautiful. When customers see what we make, they start looking at their own clothes differently, and that matters more than the tonnes we collect.

Interviewer: And what’s next for you?

Aisha: People keep telling me to open a big factory, but I’m not interested in growing too fast. I’d rather stay small and do things properly. What I would like is to run workshops in schools, so that children can learn to repair their own clothes.

Interviewer: Aisha Bello, thanks for talking to us.

passages.title: Notice on the door of Room 12
passages.text: Intermediate Group B: this week’s classes will be in Room 4 on the ground floor while new heating is put in here. Your teacher and lesson times stay the same.

passages.title: Email from the Student Office
passages.text: To all students: tickets for Friday’s trip to Bath are now on sale at reception. Payment is by card only. The coach leaves at 8.15 sharp and won’t wait for anyone who is late. Anna, Student Office

passages.title: Text message
passages.text: Marta – sorry, I can’t make our conversation exchange at 4 today! My dentist has moved my appointment. Could we do tomorrow at the same time instead? Same place, the library café. Let me know. Kenji

passages.title: Self-Study Centre
passages.text: Laptops can be borrowed for use in this room only. Show your student card at the desk. All laptops must be returned 15 minutes before the centre closes.

passages.title: Email from Ms Okafor
passages.text: Dear all, your writing test is next Wednesday. You will not be allowed to use dictionaries, but you can bring your own pens and a watch. Please check the noticeboard on Monday to find out which room you are in. Ms Okafor

passages.title: A – Symphony under the Stars
passages.text: The Northern Philharmonic Orchestra plays Beethoven and Tchaikovsky in Roundhay Park, finishing with fireworks over the lake. Bring a blanket and a picnic. The concert starts at 9 pm and ends shortly after 11. All tickets cost £25, and there are no reduced prices for children or students. If it rains, the concert will go ahead anyway.

passages.title: B – Blue Note Supper Club
passages.text: Enjoy a three-course dinner while the Ruth Adebayo Quartet plays jazz favourites from the 1950s and 60s. Our chef uses fresh local produce, and there is always a vegetarian choice. Tables are for two to eight people, so it’s perfect for celebrations. Book early for Friday and Saturday evenings, as they sell out quickly.

passages.title: C – The Snow Queen
passages.text: Hans Christian Andersen’s classic story is told with beautiful puppets, music and lights. Performances are daily at 11 am and 3 pm. The audience is asked to stay in their seats throughout, but after every show the puppeteers come out to explain how the puppets work and answer questions. Suitable for ages four and up.

passages.title: D – City Chamber Orchestra
passages.text: An evening of Mozart and Haydn in the lovely setting of St Andrew’s Church. The concert begins at 7 pm and finishes at about 8.45, with no interval. Adult tickets are £16, and students pay half price on showing a valid card. Seats are not numbered, so arrive early to get a good view.

passages.title: E – Behind the Curtain
passages.text: This clever comedy, written last year by local writer Joe Kirwan, follows a small theatre company on the night when everything goes wrong. It runs from Tuesday to Saturday. After Thursday’s performance, the cast will stay on stage to answer questions from the audience. Tickets cost £18, and the play lasts two hours.

passages.title: F – The Cellar Sessions
passages.text: Every Friday, three young jazz bands from the city’s music college play in the cellar bar of the Grand Hotel. It’s standing room only, and things get lively when the musicians start improvising. The bar serves drinks but no food, so eat before you come. Entry is £7 on the door.

passages.title: G – Jungle Beats
passages.text: A lively musical show for children aged three to eight, with performances on Saturday and Sunday at 2 pm. Young members of the audience are invited onto the stage to play drums, shake rattles and dance with the performers. The show lasts fifty minutes, and adults and children pay the same price.

passages.title: H – Laugh Out Loud
passages.text: Five of the country’s best new comedians try out fresh material every Monday night at the Old Fire Station. Some of it works and some of it doesn’t, which is half the fun. Tickets are just £8, or £6 if you book online. Some of the jokes may not suit anyone under sixteen.

passages.title: On her toes: an interview with Isla Mackenzie
passages.text:
Isla Mackenzie is seventeen and comes from Glasgow, and last month she won a place at a famous dance school in London. We asked her about her life so far.

When did you start dancing?
I started when I was six. My older sister went to ballet classes, and I had to wait for her every Saturday until her class finished. I watched through the window and copied all the steps that the older girls did. One day the teacher noticed me and invited me in. My sister stopped after a year, but I never did.

Was ballet always your favourite?
No, it wasn’t at first. To be honest, I found it quite boring as a child because there were so many rules. Then, when I was eleven, I tried contemporary dance, which felt much freer. Suddenly I understood the point of ballet. It gives you strength and control. Now I do both styles.

How much do you train?
About twenty hours a week. I go to school as normal, and then I dance every evening and on Saturdays as well. My friends often go to the cinema while I’m training. That used to upset me, but now I accept it. I see them on Sundays, and they come to all my shows.

Have you ever wanted to give up?
Only once, when I was fourteen. I hurt my ankle badly and couldn’t dance for four months. I felt completely lost because dancing was my whole life. My physiotherapist gave me exercises that I did every day. During that time I started to watch other dancers more carefully. I noticed small details in their movements. Strangely, I came back a better dancer.

How did the audition for the London school go when you finally went there?
I was terribly nervous because there were three hundred people for only thirty places. First we did a ballet class, and then we each performed a short piece. I chose a contemporary piece by my own teacher. In the middle I slipped slightly, but I didn’t stop. I just carried on and smiled. Afterwards one of the judges told me that she liked that moment the most. In her opinion, it showed my character.

What are you worried about?
Moving away from home, mostly, because I’ve never lived alone, and I can’t cook at all! My mum is giving me lessons this summer so that I don’t starve. London is expensive too, so money is a bit of a worry. Luckily, I’ve got a grant that pays for the fees.

What would you say to young people who want to dance?
Dance because you love it, not for fame. Most dancers never become stars, and that’s fine. The joy is in the dancing itself.

passages.title: From the sofa to the finish line
passages.text:
Two years ago, Owen Price could not run for a bus. The 45-year-old taxi driver from Cardiff spent most of his day sitting down, and he hardly ever did any exercise. (1) ________ His doctor told him that his blood pressure was too high and that he needed to become more active.

Owen decided to start with something small. He downloaded a free app that mixed one minute of running with ninety seconds of walking. (2) ________ After nine weeks, however, he could run for thirty minutes without stopping, and he felt prouder than he had felt for years.

That was when his daughter, Carys, suggested a marathon. Owen laughed at first. (3) ________ However, Carys had already found a six-month training plan for beginners. It started with three short runs a week and slowly added longer runs at weekends.

The plan was not always easy to follow. In January, the weather was terrible and Owen caught a bad cold. (4) ________ Instead of giving up, he went back to shorter runs for a fortnight until he felt strong again.

On race day, the crowds along the streets were enormous. Owen remembered the advice from Carys and started slowly. (5) ________ He finished in five hours and twelve minutes, and Carys was waiting at the finish line with a cup of tea. Now he wants to run the race again next year and beat his own time.

passages.title: My summer at the bookshop
passages.text: The summer I turned sixteen, I got my first job, in a small bookshop in the town centre. I saw a notice in the window and (1) ______ for it that same afternoon. The owner, Mrs Hughes, (2) ______ me a few questions about myself and then told me I could start the (3) ______ Saturday. I was delighted, but also a bit worried because I had never worked before. On my first day I had to (4) ______ a green shirt with the name of the shop on it, and I spent the morning learning how to (5) ______ the till. It was much more complicated than it looked! During the first week I (6) ______ lots of mistakes. Once I gave a customer change for twenty pounds when she had paid with a ten, and another time I put all the cookery books in the travel section. Mrs Hughes was always patient, though, and the other staff helped me whenever the shop got busy. Earning my own money made me feel much more independent, and I am going back next summer.

passages.title: Meeting Isla at last
passages.text: Four years ago, my English teacher organised an online exchange with a school in Edinburgh. Every student in our class was given a partner to write to, and mine was a girl (1) ______ name was Isla. At first I was not very keen (2) ______ the idea, because I have never enjoyed writing long messages. But the emails from Isla were so funny that I always replied straight away. Soon we were chatting by video every weekend, (3) ______ though we had never met. Last July my parents finally agreed to take me to Scotland. On the train I felt nervous, and (4) ______ worried me most was that we would have nothing to say to each other face to face. In fact, (5) ______ was no reason to worry at all. Isla was waiting on the platform holding a big sign with my name on it, and we started talking at once. I stayed with her family for a week and even had a little room of my (6) ______ at the top of the house. Now we are planning her visit to my town next spring.

passages.title: Recording 1
passages.text:
Man: Is that a new phone case?
Woman: Yes. I dropped my phone last week, so I thought I’d better protect it. Luckily the screen didn’t break, and the battery’s fine too. The only problem is that the camera doesn’t work any more, and I need it for my photography course.
Man: You should take it to the repair shop on Market Street. They’re really quick.

passages.title: Recording 2
passages.text:
Woman: Hello, I’m calling about my laptop. You were going to look at the keyboard.
Man: Yes. I’m afraid we can’t repair it, so we’ll need to put a new one in. Normally that’s seventy-five pounds altogether, sixty for the keyboard and fifteen for the work. But because you bought the laptop here, we won’t charge for the work.
Woman: So it’ll be sixty pounds?
Man: Less than that, actually. There’s fifteen pounds off all keyboards this month, so it’s just forty-five.
Woman: Great. Please go ahead.

passages.title: Recording 3
passages.text:
Woman: Have you found your tablet?
Man: Yes, thank goodness. I was sure I’d left it on the bus, so I phoned the bus company, but they didn’t have it. Then I remembered I’d used it in the café after I left the library.
Woman: And it was there?
Man: Yes. The waiter had kept it behind the counter for me.

passages.title: Recording 4
passages.text:
Man: So which one are you going to get?
Woman: I really liked the small laptop, but the screen’s too small for my design work.
Man: And the tablet with the keyboard? You could take it anywhere.
Woman: I don’t need to take it anywhere. I always work at home. So I’m going for the desktop computer. It’s got a huge screen, and it’s cheaper too.

passages.title: Recording 5
passages.text: Woman: Hello, this is Sarah from Fastline Broadband with a message for Mr Patel. You booked an engineer to look at your internet connection tomorrow at nine o’clock. I’m afraid he’s ill, so another engineer will come instead. She’s busy until half past eleven, so she can’t come in the morning, but she’ll be with you at two o’clock. Please call us back if that time is a problem.

passages.title: Recording 6
passages.text:
Man: Excuse me, do you sell chargers for this phone?
Woman: Yes, they’re over there, next to the phone cases.
Man: Great. I left mine at my hotel. Oh, and have you got any earphones?
Woman: Sorry, we’ve sold out. We’ll have more on Friday.
Man: Never mind. I’ll just take the charger, then.

passages.title: Recording 7
passages.text:
Man: How was your computer course?
Woman: Really good. I wanted to learn how to make a website for my business, but that course was full, so I did the one on photos instead. Now I can make all my holiday pictures look professional.
Man: Maybe you could do the website course next term.
Woman: Yes, I will. My son also wants me to try making computer games with him, but I don’t think so!

passages.title: Dialogue 1
passages.text:
Man: Have you seen the little brown bin the council left for food waste?
Woman: Yes, and I was ready to hate it. I thought the whole kitchen would smell.
Man: And does it?
Woman: Not at all. The lid closes really tightly. And our ordinary bin’s half empty now, so we only take the rubbish out once a week. Honestly, it’s made life easier.
Man: Hmm. I’m still not sure it’s worth all the trouble.

passages.title: Dialogue 2
passages.text:
Man: That’s a great jacket. Is it new?
Woman: No, it’s second-hand, from the charity shop on Church Street.
Man: Really? You love that seventies look, don’t you?
Woman: Not especially. This one just fitted me. I used to buy new clothes all the time, but then I watched a programme about how many clothes get thrown away every year. Millions of tonnes! So now I try not to buy anything new.
Man: It must save you money too.
Woman: Not always. Some of those shops aren’t cheap. But that isn’t why I do it.

passages.title: Dialogue 3
passages.text:
Woman: Did you get the letter from the school about plastic bottles?
Man: Yes. From next month the children have to bring metal ones instead.
Woman: I think it’s a good idea, but the school should give them one each. Not every family can pay fifteen pounds for a bottle.
Man: You’re right. That’s the real problem.
Woman: Mind you, my son Leo will probably lose his in a week.
Man: Oh, I don’t think so. My daughter’s had the same lunch box for three years.

passages.title: Dialogue 4
passages.text:
Woman: Do you really cycle to work every day now?
Man: Since March. I only started because my car broke down and I didn’t want to pay for the repair straight away.
Woman: Isn’t it dangerous on the main road?
Man: There’s a cycle path most of the way, so I feel quite safe. And it’s only five minutes slower than driving, with all the traffic. The funny thing is, I actually look forward to it now. I never thought I’d say that!

passages.title: Dialogue 5
passages.text:
Man: How was the beach clean-up on Saturday?
Woman: Really well organised. They gave us gloves and bags, and there were about forty of us. But what shocked me was how much of the rubbish was plastic packaging, exactly like the stuff I buy every week.
Man: Really?
Woman: Since then I’ve been taking my own containers to the market and buying fruit without any packaging. I’ll never look at a supermarket shelf in the same way again.

passages.title: Dialogue 6
passages.text:
Woman: You’re going to Edinburgh by train? From Cornwall? That’s nine hours!
Man: I know. And it cost more than the plane, too.
Woman: So why? Are you scared of flying?
Man: No, I fly for work all the time. But I read how much pollution one flight makes, and I felt terrible. This time I wanted to travel in a way that’s better for the planet. And I’ll get lots of reading done.

passages.title: River Wendle Clean-Up Day
passages.text:
Woman: Hi everyone, I’m Ruth, and I’m organising this year’s River Wendle Clean-Up Day, which is happening on Sunday the fourteenth of May. Thanks for coming to this meeting. Let me tell you what you need to know.

We’ll all meet in the car park next to the old mill, at the bottom of Station Road. Please don’t go to the bridge in the town centre. That’s where we met last year, but there’s building work there at the moment.

The poster says we’re starting at ten o’clock, but that was a mistake, I’m afraid. We’ll actually start at half past nine, so please try to arrive a few minutes before that.

As for equipment, we’ll give everyone rubbish bags and litter pickers, those long grabbers, so you won’t need to bring those. What you do need to bring is a pair of gloves. Strong ones, please, because there can be broken glass near the water. And wear old clothes, as you’re going to get muddy.

You might be wondering what we find. Mostly it’s plastic bottles and cans, of course, and every year there are a couple of shopping trolleys. But the strangest thing we pulled out last year was a guitar. It was in surprisingly good condition, actually!

At about one o’clock we’ll stop for lunch. The café by the river has closed down, unfortunately, but a local bakery has kindly offered to bring sandwiches and cakes for everyone, free of charge.

Finally, families are very welcome. Children aged fourteen and over can come on their own, but anyone under fourteen must be with an adult. Last year the age was twelve, but we’ve changed it because some parts of the riverbank are quite steep.

If you have any questions, you can find me after the meeting. See you on the fourteenth!

passages.title: Interview with a young climber
passages.text:
Interviewer: I’m here with seventeen-year-old Leo Hartley, who has just been chosen for the national youth climbing team. Leo, how did you get into climbing?

Leo: It was because of my older sister, really. She went to a climbing wall for a friend’s birthday party and loved it, and the next week I went along with her, just because I was bored. I wasn’t sporty at all. I was terrible at football, so I didn’t expect much. But after ten minutes on the wall I knew I’d found my thing.

Interviewer: What is it about climbing that you enjoy most?

Leo: People think it’s all about being strong, and you do need strength. But for me the best part is the puzzle. Every route is different, and you have to work out where to put your hands and feet. When you finally manage a route you’ve been stuck on for weeks, it’s an amazing feeling.

Interviewer: Do you prefer climbing indoors or outdoors?

Leo: Competitions are all indoors, so I train on climbing walls most of the time, and they’re great for practising. But nothing compares to being on real rock in the mountains. The views, the quiet… Whenever I can, I go to Wales with my coach.

Interviewer: Is climbing dangerous?

Leo: Everyone asks that! My mum worried a lot at first. But honestly, with the right equipment and a good partner, it’s much safer than most people imagine. Accidents usually happen when people get careless, so I always check everything twice.

Interviewer: How do you manage school and training?

Leo: It isn’t easy. I train five evenings a week, so I do my homework on the bus and at lunchtime. My teachers have been really understanding, though. When I had a competition in France, they sent me work to do so that I didn’t fall behind.

Interviewer: What are your hopes for the future?

Leo: Lots of people expect me to say the Olympics. That would be incredible, of course, but I try not to think that far ahead. Right now I just want to keep enjoying it. If I stop having fun, there’s no point.

Interviewer: Leo, good luck.

passages.title: Pawsworth Veterinary Surgery
passages.text: Please keep dogs on a short lead and cats in a closed basket while you are in the waiting room. If your pet is nervous of other animals, tell reception and we will find you a quieter place to wait.

passages.title: Fish food – special offer
passages.text: Buy two large tubs of fish food and get a free water-testing kit. Offer ends Saturday or while kits last. Ask a member of staff to help you choose the right food for your fish.

passages.title: Text message from Greenway Vets
passages.text: Hi Mrs Doyle, Biscuit’s operation went well and she is awake now. You can collect her this afternoon any time after 3. She mustn’t eat anything until this evening, and only a little then. Call us if you have any questions. Greenway Vets

passages.title: Puppy training classes
passages.text: Saturdays, 10–11 am, in the hall behind the shop. Puppies must be between 10 and 20 weeks old and must have had all their injections. Places are limited, so book at the till.

passages.title: Notice to clients
passages.text: From next month, the surgery will be closed on Wednesday afternoons. For emergencies at these times, please call our partner clinic in Hillbrook on 01632 960418, which is open 24 hours a day.

passages.title: A – Tourist Information Centre, Edinburgh
passages.text: Join our friendly team at the desk on the Royal Mile, answering visitors’ questions and helping them book tours and hotels. Speakers of a second language such as French, Spanish or Italian are especially welcome. Shifts run from 8 am to 1 pm, Monday to Friday, from June to the end of August.

passages.title: B – Pets Corner, Bristol
passages.text: Our busy pet shop needs a summer assistant to serve customers, clean the cages and feed the rabbits, birds and fish. Most of the work is indoors, and you will spend a lot of time on the till. Applicants must live within easy reach of the shop, as we cannot help with accommodation.

passages.title: C – Sunshine Sports Camp, Cardiff
passages.text: We need coaches to run football, tennis and swimming sessions for children aged seven to twelve. You must hold a lifeguard certificate to work in the pool, and experience with young people is useful. Hours are 9 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, for six weeks. Lunch is provided for all staff.

passages.title: D – Open-top Bus Guide, York
passages.text: Ride around the city on our famous red buses and tell passengers about York’s long history. Tours are in English, but guides who can repeat the main points in another language get extra pay. Full training is given. Tours run every hour from 2 pm until the last one leaves at 8 pm.

passages.title: E – Hilltop Farm Park, Cumbria
passages.text: Help feed the goats, sheep and rabbits, and show visitors around the fields. You’ll be outside in all weathers, so bring a good coat! Staff who live more than an hour away can stay free of charge in the farm’s cottage, which has its own kitchen. Applicants must be at least sixteen.

passages.title: F – Little Artists Holiday Club, Norwich
passages.text: Help children aged four to seven with painting, model-making and other craft activities in our bright studio. An interest in art is more important than experience. The club runs from 9 am to 2.30 pm, so you’ll have your afternoons free. Work as many weeks as you like between July and September.

passages.title: G – Seaview Hotel Kitchen, Cornwall
passages.text: Kitchen assistants are needed to prepare breakfasts and help our chefs at lunchtime. Our pay is well above the usual rate for this kind of work, with extra for weekend shifts. Free meals for all staff. This is full-time work only: 40 hours a week from early July to the middle of September.

passages.title: H – The Corner Café, Brighton
passages.text: Our small seaside café is looking for someone to make sandwiches, bake cakes and serve customers. You’ll learn a lot from our cook, who trained in Paris. The pay is the minimum rate, but tips are shared equally. We only need help at weekends, so this would suit someone who is studying.

passages.title: The kitchen scientist
passages.text:
Every Sunday afternoon, sixteen-year-old Priya Shah turns her family’s kitchen in Cardiff into a science laboratory. She puts her phone on a pile of books and starts filming while her parents are out. Her short videos explain everyday science, such as the reason bread rises or ice floats. Her channel, Kitchen Lab, now has more than 80,000 subscribers.

Priya never planned to become a video maker. Two years ago she was having problems with chemistry at school. Her textbook seemed dull, and the diagrams meant nothing to her. One evening she tried an experiment from the book at home, with vinegar and baking soda. Suddenly the reaction made sense. Her cousin was having the same problem with chemistry, so she filmed the next experiment for him. He shared it with his class, and soon strangers were asking for more.

The first videos were not very good because the sound was poor, and Priya talked too fast. Some viewers left unkind comments. “I nearly deleted everything after the first month,” she admits. Her older brother persuaded her to continue. He bought her a cheap microphone and showed her how to edit. Now each video takes about six hours to make. Most of that time goes on research. “I check every fact in at least two places. A mistake in a science video is worse than no video at all.”

Safety is important to her too, so she never uses dangerous chemicals. Every experiment uses things from an ordinary kitchen. At the start of each video, she reminds younger viewers to ask an adult for help.

Her chemistry teacher, Mr Evans, is a big fan who sometimes shows her videos in his lessons. “Priya explains things in the language of teenagers,” he says. “Students listen to her in a different way. They listen to me because they have to!”

Success has brought some surprises. Last spring a university invited her to speak at a science festival. She was terrified of the large audience, but she enjoyed it in the end. Companies have also offered her money to advertise their products. So far she has said no to all of them. “My viewers trust me. I don’t want them to think I’m selling something.”

Priya wants to study medicine, so she is not sure about the future of Kitchen Lab. “Maybe I’ll stop, maybe I won’t. For now, it’s fun, and I’m learning more than my viewers!”

passages.title: Six pupils and one teacher
passages.text:
On the island of Inchmara, off the west coast of Scotland, there is a primary school with just six pupils. They are between five and eleven years old, and they all learn together in one classroom. (1) ________ Fiona MacLeod has worked at the school for nine years, and she says that she would never change her job.

Teaching children of such different ages is not simple. Every morning, Fiona gives each pupil a plan for the day. (2) ________ The older ones often help the younger ones with their reading, and this is good for both groups.

The island has no shops apart from a small post office, and the ferry to the mainland only sails three times a week. (3) ________ Instead, the children use the island itself as a classroom. In science lessons, they study the birds on the cliffs, and in maths they measure the height of the waves.

Some people worry that the children do not have enough friends of their own age. (4) ________ Twice a term, the pupils take the ferry to a larger school on the mainland and spend the day with children of the same age. They also have a video call every week with a small school in Norway.

The biggest problem for the school is its future. Two of the pupils will leave for secondary school next summer, and only one new child is expected. (5) ________ But Fiona is hopeful. Several young families have moved to the island recently, because they can now work from home online.

passages.title: A weekend with the birds
passages.text: My grandfather has loved birds all his life, and last April he (1) ______ me to spend a weekend bird watching with him in Norfolk. On the first morning we got up at five o’clock and walked to a small wooden hut beside a lake. Inside, we sat on a narrow bench and tried not to (2) ______ any noise, because even a cough can frighten birds away. For a long time nothing happened, and I started to feel cold and bored. Then, after about an hour, I suddenly (3) ______ sight of a flash of bright blue above the water. It was a kingfisher! It moved so fast that I was amazed when I (4) ______ to take a photo of it. Grandad was delighted. He (5) ______ a notebook in which he writes down every bird he sees, and he let me add the kingfisher to his list. By the end of the weekend we had seen thirty-two different kinds of birds. I never expected to enjoy it so much, but now I have (6) ______ up bird watching myself.

passages.title: Not quite a birthday feast
passages.text: Last month my father turned fifty, and I offered to cook a special dinner for the whole family. I had watched lots of cooking programmes, so I was sure it would be easy. How wrong I was! First, I found out that we did not have (1) ______ eggs at all, so I had to run to the corner shop. While I was out, the cheese sauce boiled for (2) ______ long that it turned into a thick brown paste. Then I added salt to the rice twice by mistake, and it became (3) ______ salty for anyone to eat. When Dad came home, the kitchen was full of smoke and there was nothing on the table at all, apart (4) ______ a plate of burnt bread. Luckily, he just laughed. We opened all the windows and walked to the little Italian restaurant (5) ______ my parents had their first date many years ago. The pizza was delicious. Afterwards, (6) ______ took us nearly two hours to clean the kitchen, but Dad said it was the most memorable birthday he had ever had.

passages.title: Recording 1
passages.text:
Woman: Good morning, Tom. I know you usually start by checking the emails, but can you leave them until later today? The delivery’s coming at ten, and the storeroom’s in a terrible mess. Could you sort that out first?
Man: Of course. And what about Mrs Green? She wanted someone to call her back.
Woman: Don’t worry, I’ll phone her myself.

passages.title: Recording 2
passages.text:
Man: Is the team meeting still in Meeting Room Two this afternoon?
Woman: No, there’s a problem with the heating in there. It’s freezing.
Man: We could go to the café downstairs.
Woman: It’s too noisy. Let’s use the staff kitchen. There’s a big table, and nobody uses it after lunch.
Man: OK, I’ll tell everyone.

passages.title: Recording 3
passages.text:
Man: I heard you’ve left the hospital.
Woman: Yes. After eight years as a nurse, I wanted a change. I thought about teaching, but you need another year of training for that.
Man: So what are you doing now?
Woman: I’m working on reception at the Park Hotel. I love meeting people from all over the world.

passages.title: Recording 4
passages.text:
Woman: Are you on the afternoon shift again next week, Dan?
Man: No. I’ve been doing two o’clock starts for a month now, so they’ve moved me. Next week I’m on the early shift.
Woman: Eight o’clock? That’s not too bad.
Man: I wish! The early shift starts at six now. I’ll have to get up at five.

passages.title: Recording 5
passages.text:
Woman: Hi, are you the engineer? The printer on this floor isn’t working.
Man: Actually, I’m here for the photocopier. Your office manager called us this morning.
Woman: Oh, the photocopier? I didn’t know that was broken too.
Man: Yes, it’s making a strange noise, apparently. I’m afraid I don’t do printers. You’ll need to call a different company for that.
Woman: And I don’t suppose you can do anything about the coffee machine either!

passages.title: Recording 6
passages.text:
Man: So, we’ll see you on Monday at nine. Have you got everything you need?
Woman: I think so. Do I need to bring my passport?
Man: No, we saw that at the interview. And we’ll take your photo for your ID card here. But we haven’t got your bank details yet, so please bring those, or we can’t pay you!
Woman: Of course. I’ll bring them with me.

passages.title: Recording 7
passages.text:
Man: What’s it like working at the park?
Woman: It’s great. In summer I spend most of the day cutting the grass, which gets a bit boring. Sometimes visitors stop and ask me questions, and that’s nice. But the best part is in autumn, when we plant new trees. It’s hard work, but I know they’ll still be there in a hundred years.

passages.title: Dialogue 1
passages.text:
Man: I thought you wanted a kitten.
Woman: So did I! The rescue centre had lots of them. But the staff told me kittens are full of energy and climb all over the furniture. I work from home, and I need peace and quiet for that. Biscuit’s nine, and she just sleeps on the chair next to my desk all day.
Man: Was she cheaper than a kitten?
Woman: No, it was the same price, actually.

passages.title: Dialogue 2
passages.text:
Woman: How are the training classes going with Rocky?
Man: Better than I hoped. I thought the trainer would just teach Rocky to sit, but really she teaches the owners. Most of the problems were my fault. I was giving him treats at the wrong time!
Woman: Aren’t those classes expensive?
Man: Twenty pounds each, but they’re worth it. And Rocky’s only one, so he learns fast.

passages.title: Dialogue 3
passages.text:
Woman: Well, what did you think of the wildlife park?
Man: The animals looked healthy, and they had loads of space. Not like the old zoo in town.
Woman: True. The keepers obviously care about them. But the café was a disaster. Twenty minutes for a sandwich!
Man: I didn’t mind that. What I didn’t like was the price. Thirty pounds each is too much.
Woman: Hmm, for a whole day out, I think it’s fair.

passages.title: Dialogue 4
passages.text:
Woman: Every Saturday at the dog shelter? That’s kind of you.
Man: It isn’t that kind, really. I’ve always wanted a dog, but pets aren’t allowed in my flat. This way I get to spend time with dogs without breaking the rules.
Woman: And you must get fit, walking all those dogs.
Man: I already run every day, so that’s not the point.
Woman: Have you ever thought of working with animals?
Man: Not seriously. I’m happy in my job.

passages.title: Dialogue 5
passages.text:
Man: How’s your daughter’s rabbit?
Woman: Well, she begged for him for a year and promised she’d look after him. For the first month she did. Now guess who cleans the cage every Sunday?
Man: You?
Woman: Me! But the strange thing is, I don’t mind at all. I sit with him in the garden in the evenings, and he’s really become my rabbit too. I’m quite glad she wanted one.

passages.title: Dialogue 6
passages.text:
Woman: Did you watch that programme about foxes last night?
Man: I did. I used to think foxes were just a nuisance. One keeps opening our bins.
Woman: Me too.
Man: But I feel differently now. It showed how clever they are, and how hard it is for them to raise their cubs in a city. There was one sad bit when a cub got lost, but it found its mother in the end.
Woman: I fell asleep before the end. It was an hour and a half!
Man: I didn’t notice the time at all.

passages.title: Opening day at the Westgate Shopping Centre
passages.text:
Man: Good afternoon. I’m David Moss, manager of the new Westgate Shopping Centre, and I’d like to tell you about our opening day this Saturday.

The doors will open at nine o’clock, and at ten the centre will be officially opened by a well-known footballer who grew up here in Northfield. There were stories in the local paper that a famous singer was coming, but I’m afraid that isn’t true.

So, what will you find inside? On Saturday there will be sixty-five shops open, on three floors. We had hoped to have seventy by the opening day, but a few aren’t quite ready yet, so those will open later in the year.

On the top floor there’s a cinema with six screens, and next to it a food court with restaurants from all over the world. We’re also planning a bowling alley, but that won’t be finished until next summer.

Getting here is easy. Our car park has space for a thousand cars, and parking is free for the first two hours. After that it costs one pound an hour. If you’d rather leave the car at home, the number forty-two bus stops right outside the main entrance. The number twenty-four also comes to this part of town, but it stops on the other side of the river, which is quite a long walk.

And finally, a little gift. Lots of new shopping centres give away shopping bags on their opening day, but we thought we’d do something different. So the first hundred customers through the door will each get a free umbrella, in our special Westgate colours. Very useful in this weather!

We’re really looking forward to seeing you all on Saturday.

passages.title: Interview with a young drummer
passages.text:
Interviewer: Today I’m talking to Jess Moran, who’s nineteen and plays the drums in the band Paper Lanterns. Their first album came out last month. Jess, how did the band start?

Jess: We all met at college in Brighton. Sam, our singer, put a note on the noticeboard asking for a drummer, and I almost didn’t reply, because I didn’t think I was good enough. My best friend made me go to the first practice. I’m so glad she did.

Interviewer: What was it like recording your first album?

Jess: Harder than I expected. On stage, if you make a small mistake, nobody notices because everyone’s dancing. In the studio, you have to play the same song again and again until it’s perfect. Some days I got really fed up. But it taught me a lot about being patient.

Interviewer: Do you all agree about the kind of music you want to make?

Jess: Not at all! We argue about it all the time. Sam likes slow, sad songs and I prefer something you can dance to. But actually, I think that’s why our music works. If we all wanted the same thing, it would be boring.

Interviewer: Lots of bands become famous online these days. How do you feel about social media?

Jess: It’s useful, I can’t deny that. Most of our fans found us through videos online. But I don’t enjoy it. I’d much rather spend my time writing music than thinking about what to post every day. Luckily, our bass player loves doing it.

Interviewer: What’s your favourite thing about being in a band?

Jess: People expect me to say the big concerts, and they are fun. But for me it’s the small gigs in tiny clubs, where you can see everyone’s faces and chat to them afterwards. That’s when you really feel close to the audience.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to young musicians?

Jess: Practise, obviously. But more than that, play with other people as often as you can. You can practise alone in your bedroom for years, but you only really improve when you have to listen to other musicians.

Interviewer: Jess Moran, thank you.

passages.title: Note under a door
passages.text: To whoever lives in Flat 6 – a parcel for you was left with me on Tuesday because you were out. I’m at work during the day, so please knock after 6 pm to collect it. Joe, Flat 2

passages.title: Lift out of order
passages.text: An engineer is coming to repair the lift on Thursday morning. Until then, residents with heavy shopping or pushchairs can ask the caretaker, Mr Patel, for help. His number is on the board by the main entrance.

passages.title: Bike store – residents only
passages.text: Lock all bikes to the rails. Any bike without a Brookfield House sticker will be removed after 31 May. Stickers are free from the management office.

passages.title: Email from Harlow Property Management
passages.text: Dear residents, the water will be turned off on Monday 9 June between 9 am and 1 pm while old pipes are replaced. Please fill a few bottles the night before. We are sorry for any problems this may cause.

passages.title: Message on the residents’ group chat
passages.text: Hi everyone! I’m Lena and I’ve just moved into Flat 11. I’m having a small get-together on Saturday from 4 pm to say hello – drinks and cake in the garden. Children welcome. If it rains, we’ll move into the entrance hall.

passages.title: A – The Long Lunch
passages.text: Famous chefs chat about their favourite restaurants around the world over a long, relaxed meal. The conversations are lively and fast, with lots of jokes and people talking over each other. Episodes often last more than an hour, and a full written transcript of each one is available on our website the following day.

passages.title: B – Kitchen on a Budget
passages.text: Every week, chef Sam Price shows you how to make a tasty dinner for two for under £5, using ingredients from any supermarket. Episodes last about fifteen minutes, which makes them perfect for listening to on the way to work or college. The full recipes, with shopping lists, are on the website.

passages.title: C – Slow English Travels
passages.text: Each week, presenter Kate Morris visits a different British city and describes what she sees, eats and hears there. She speaks slowly and clearly, choosing everyday words, so the podcast is ideal for learners of English. The full text of every episode can be downloaded free, so you can read along while you listen.

passages.title: D – Run With Us
passages.text: Runners of every level, from complete beginners to Olympic athletes, share their training tips and talk about how they felt before their first race. Each episode is planned to last exactly thirty minutes, the same as an easy run, so you can listen with your headphones in while you’re out on the road.

passages.title: E – History Hour
passages.text: Two university professors spend an hour discussing a different period of history each week, from ancient Egypt to the Second World War. They often disagree, which makes for an interesting discussion, and listeners can send in questions for them to answer. A list of books for further reading is posted after every episode.

passages.title: F – Why Is the Sky Blue?
passages.text: Each week, two comedians ask a top scientist a simple question about the world and try to understand the answer. The jokes come thick and fast, but you’ll learn something real too. The show is suitable for the whole family, and children often send in questions that are used in later episodes.

passages.title: G – Body Matters
passages.text: Dr Helen Achebe explains the science behind how our bodies work, from how muscles grow during exercise to why we need sleep. Each episode looks at the latest research in detail and is aimed at adults who want serious, reliable information. It’s best listened to at home, when you can concentrate and take notes.

passages.title: H – Voices from the Past
passages.text: Actors bring real events from history to life, from the building of the pyramids to the first flight across the Atlantic. Each episode is a short radio play with music and sound effects, so you feel as if you are really there. A new story is released every Friday, and older episodes are all free.

passages.title: 312 bottles: how our school changed
passages.text:
Amara Okafor, fifteen, explains how her school cut its plastic waste.

Last year I counted the plastic bottles in the bins at my school in Plymouth. It took me a whole lunch break. In one day there were 312 bottles, and almost none of them were recycled. That number shocked me so much that it became the start of our project.

At first I tried to do everything alone. I put a cardboard box in the canteen with a sign: “Bottles here, please”. After a week the box was full of crisp packets, apple cores and chewing gum. I felt like giving up. My form tutor, Ms Hughes, had a different idea. “People don’t change because of a box,” she told me. “They change because their friends do.”

So I asked for volunteers. Six students from different year groups joined me, and we called ourselves the Green Team. Each of us talked to our own class about what we had found. We also made a short film about the bottles and showed it in assembly. The younger students loved it, but some older ones laughed at us. That was hard. For a few days I felt quite embarrassed in the corridors.

Next we needed proper recycling bins. The head teacher liked the idea, but there was no money for them. We organised a cake sale and a sponsored walk along the coast. Together they raised £650, enough for ten bins. A local company that collects rubbish agreed to empty them for free every week.

The bins helped, but the biggest change came from the water fountains. Two fountains in the school had been broken for months. We wrote a letter to the head teacher, and they were repaired. We also sold metal water bottles with the school badge on them. Now most students fill up their own bottle. They no longer buy a new one every day.

This year we counted again. On an average day there are fewer than forty plastic bottles, and nearly all of them go into the recycling bins. Other schools in the city have asked us for advice. In May we even gave a talk at a meeting for local teachers.

People often ask me about the lessons of the project. For me, the people are more important than the numbers. A project like this needs a team. I am quite shy, and I could never speak in assembly on my own. Working with others gave me confidence. Next year I want to start on food waste. It will be harder, but I am not worried because our team is bigger now.

passages.title: The Cornish pasty: a lunch with a handle
passages.text:
Today you can buy a Cornish pasty at almost any railway station in Britain, but this famous snack began as a working lunch. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, thousands of men worked in the tin and copper mines of Cornwall, in the far south-west of England. (1) ________ They needed a meal that was filling, easy to carry and still warm several hours later.

The pasty was the perfect answer. It is made from a circle of pastry, folded over a filling of beef, potato, onion and a vegetable called swede. (2) ________ According to a popular story, the miners held the pasty by this thick edge, because their hands were often dirty. They ate the rest and threw the crust away.

Some families had their own special recipes, and some pasties even had meat at one end and fruit at the other. (3) ________ That way, each man knew which pasty was his, even when they were all kept warm together.

When the mines started to close in the late nineteenth century, many Cornish miners moved abroad to find work. (4) ________ As a result, you can still find pasties today in parts of Mexico, Australia and the United States.

In 2011, the Cornish pasty received special protection from the European Union. (5) ________ It must also have the famous D shape, with the crimp on one side. For the people of Cornwall, this was an important way to protect a piece of their history.

passages.title: Sunday at the flea market
passages.text: Every Sunday morning, the car park behind our town hall (1) ______ into a lively flea market. Around eighty sellers put out tables covered with old books, toys, clothes, records and kitchen things. If you arrive early and look carefully, you can often find a real (2) ______. Last month I went along with my cousin Tom, who (3) ______ old cameras and already owns more than forty of them. He told me that the prices written on the labels are never final. Sellers usually (4) ______ you to ask for a lower price, and some of them seem disappointed if you do not. Tom is very good at this. After chatting to one woman for ten minutes, he bought a camera from the 1960s in perfect (5) ______ for half of what she had asked at first. I am not as patient as Tom, so I just (6) ______ two pounds on a pile of old comics and went to get a hot drink. Still, I had a great morning, and I am planning to go back next week with a list of things to look for.

passages.title: The Riverside Rovers
passages.text: My family moved to Leeds last year, and I knew nobody there. My dad suggested joining a local football team. The Riverside Rovers had a terrible reputation: the season before, they had lost (1) ______ single match. I joined anyway. The coach, a retired PE teacher called Mr Okafor, believed that hard work mattered more than talent. In my first training session he spent an hour teaching us (2) ______ to pass the ball without looking at our feet. He also made us promise never to let the rest of the team (3) ______ by missing training without a good reason. Slowly, things began to improve. Nobody missed a single session all winter, (4) ______ though the weather was often freezing. In our last match of the season we played the team that had beaten us 7–0 in September. At half-time we (5) ______ losing 2–0, and I thought nothing had changed. But in the second half we scored three goals in twenty minutes. When the final whistle blew, we ran to hug each (6) ______, laughing and shouting. Joining the Rovers was the best way to make friends in a new city.
